exactement de la Châtagne, Aicide Matthey de
l'Etang (Matthey de la Gouille, comme l'
appelaient ses amis) avait passé la majeure partie
de g. vie dans cette vallée jurassienne où dans
lés temps anciens vécurent (?) le Solitaire dès
Sagnes et Gédéon le Contreleyu. Cet endroit
avait été par lui choisi en une occasion
mémorable, quand un beau jour, ou plutôt un
malheureux soir, il s'était aventuré à demander
Êour femme la grande Uranie Montandon du
ronillet. A sa complète stupéfaction, il lui
fut répondu négativement. Quand il demanda
les raisons de ce refus, elle lui déclara tout
uniment « qu'il sentait trop l'horloger >.
Pendant une heure ou deux, l'Alcide scngea à se
noyer de dépit dans le lac des Tailleres, mais
son bon sens lui revenant ei l'instinct de
conservation aidant, il se borna à secouer sur ce
Sol ingrat la poussière de ses souliers et,
quelque temps plus tard, alla planter sa tente aux
Cœudres, pensant que son noir chagrin se
fondrait dans les brouillards de la Sagne.
Horloger de son métier, il était aussi un
enragé coureur de forêts, ramassant fruits et
champignons, à l'occasion cueillant des plantes rares
pour l'herboriste des Geneveys, ou
collectionnant toutes les curiosités des règnes animal,
minéral et végétal pour enrichir le musée du
village, où se trouven t réunis de glorieux
vestiges du bon vieux temps, où l'on était Prussiens,
voisinant avec un autographe de Victor Hugo et
des armes de Zanzibar.
Pour tout dire, Aicide Matthey était dans son
genre une personnalité intéressante et
originale, quelque peu misanthrope qui ne voyait

D aimait à parcourir tout seul les forêts des
environs ou les _pâturages de Sonmartel ou du
Mont-Racine, _monologuant et devisant sur les
gens et les choses. A part ça, homme serviable
et complaisant qui n'aurait pas fait de mal à
une mouche.

besogne habituelle, il partit vers quatre heures dans

cela sur le papier, mats de peur d'être
reconnu, il remit l'objet à sa place, le recouvrit avec
eoin et, tout songeur, prit le chemin du retour.
Et tout en redescendant, cette phrase lui
_révélait continuellement : « Un cœur, un cœur
fidèle à ton retour. _» Ne vouil ___ t pour rien au
monéâ. tomber dans ce qu'il appelait les bêtises du
_gentiment, il s'adressa intérieurement une verte
admonestation, finissant par dire tout fort :
« Eh ! bien, ça te revient, vieux curieux que tu
s ; pour une fois, tu as été bien attrapé ; çà

komxne. Fram.

completion:
The Hidden Treasure
Tales from Our Homeland

Although a native of La Brévine, or more precisely of La Châtagne, Alcide Matthey de l'Étang (Matthey de la Gouille, as his friends called him) had spent the greater part of his life in that Jura valley where in ancient times lived (?) the Hermit of the Marshes and Gédéon the Counter-Liar. This place had been chosen by him on a memorable occasion, when one fine day, or rather one unfortunate evening, he had ventured to ask for the hand of the great Uranie Montandon of Ronillet. To his complete astonishment, he received a negative reply. When he asked for the reasons for this refusal, she simply told him "that he smelled too much of the watchmaker."

For an hour or two, Alcide thought of drowning himself in despair in Lake Taillières, but as his good sense returned and the instinct of self-preservation aiding, he merely shook the dust of his shoes on that ungrateful soil and, some time later, went to pitch his tent at Les Cœudres, thinking that his dark sorrow would melt into the mists of the marsh.

A watchmaker by trade, he was also an avid wanderer of the forests, gathering fruits and mushrooms, occasionally picking rare plants for the herbalist of Les Geneveys, or collecting all manner of curiosities from the animal, mineral, and vegetable kingdoms to enrich the village museum, where glorious relics of the good old days, when they were Prussians, were displayed alongside an autograph of Victor Hugo and weapons from Zanzibar.

To put it simply, Alcide Matthey was in his own way an interesting and original personality, somewhat misanthropic, who saw in the human race only mischief and malice. He loved to roam alone through the surrounding forests or the pastures of Sonmartel or Mont Racine, monologuing and discoursing on people and things. Apart from that, a helpful and obliging man who wouldn't harm a fly.

One Saturday at the end of the year, having finished his usual work, he set out around four o'clock in the direction of Mont Racine, taking the path he knew well and which, leading straight upward, brought him near the summit. He walked briskly, looking around from time to time to see if anyone might happen to be on his path, in which case he would have preferred to make a wide detour to remain alone and free. He was soon near the wall bordering the high pastures and stopped for a moment near three fir trees to light his pipe.

This operation completed, he was about to turn left to climb to the signal, when he saw on the slope of the last ascent a peculiar figure crouching, who seemed to be searching for or digging up something. This sight greatly intrigued him, and leaning once more against his fir trees, he began to observe the stranger, a young man, fair-haired, who continued his work with ardor. What the devil is he "digging" for there? thought Alcide; has he found a gold mine? After a moment, the searcher stopped, then he seemed to examine an object he held in his hands. Five minutes later, he began to "poke" the ground again, and this time, apparently, he was filling in his hole. Good! thought the watcher, we'll go see this business up close, if he leaves. Indeed, he left, looking quite cheerful, and went back down the mountain by another path. Alcide, having waited a moment longer, went straight toward the mysterious hiding place. He easily discovered the freshly turned earth and, removing the stones, began in turn to dig. At a shallow depth, he laid his hand on a tin box which he picked up and found very light: "A bad sign," he said, "it's nothing very grand."

Without scruples, being as curious as an old maid, he opened the box, which contained a simple paper folded in four, resting on an orchid and a tuft of golden broom. He read these words on the note:

Happy is he who possesses a love,
A heart faithful upon his return.
In memory of August 28, 192*.
Zélie and Pierrot

The old bachelor was not long in understanding the story of the young lover coming here on a pilgrimage to revisit the places where, on a beautiful summer Sunday, facing the sparkling Alps, they had spent such sweet hours, happy moments of which they wanted the places themselves to keep the memory:
"...we have, in walking, left some trace,
Our heart has dreamed beneath the blue horizons."

Holding his unexpected find in his hands, our man found himself rather embarrassed at having thus penetrated the secret of this fresh idyll. But his bitterness as a suitor, long "pickled," resurfacing, he began to grumble:
"Yes, yes, all that is very fine, provided it lasts."

He even had a momentary temptation to write that on the paper, but for fear of being recognized, he put the object back in its place, covered it carefully, and, deep in thought, took the path back. And while descending, this phrase kept coming back to him: "A heart, a heart faithful upon your return." Not wanting for anything in the world to fall into what he called the foolishness of sentimentality, he inwardly gave himself a stern admonition, ending by saying aloud:
"Well, that serves you right, you old busybody; for once, you've been well caught; that will teach you not to stick your nose everywhere."

And considering this matter buried, he began to think about the morels that would surely be early this spring. He must not let his spots be stolen.

As for Zélie and Pierrot, if they went back to find their dear memories, they perhaps never suspected having thrown trouble for a moment into the heart of a good man. Fram.

A watchmaker by trade, he was also an avid wanderer of the forests, gathering fruits and mushrooms, occasionally picking rare plants for the herbalist of Les Geneveys, or collecting all manner of curiosities from the animal, mineral, and vegetable kingdoms to enrich the village museum, where glorious relics of the good old days, when they were Prussians, were displayed alongside an autograph of Victor Hugo and weapons from Zanzibar.

To put it simply, Alcide Matthey was in his own way an interesting and original personality, somewhat misanthropic, who saw in the human race only mischief and malice. He loved to roam alone through the surrounding forests or the pastures of Sonmartel or Mont Racine, monologuing and discoursing on people and things. Apart from that, a helpful and obliging man who wouldn't harm a fly.

One Saturday at the end of the year, having finished his usual work, he set out around four o'clock in the direction of Mont Racine, taking the path he knew well and which, leading straight upward, brought him near the summit. He walked briskly, looking around from time to time to see if anyone might happen to be on his path, in which case he would have preferred to make a wide detour to remain alone and free. He was soon near the wall bordering the high pastures and stopped for a moment near three fir trees to light his pipe.

This operation completed, he was about to turn left to climb to the signal, when he saw on the slope of the last ascent a peculiar figure crouching, who seemed to be searching for or digging up something. This sight greatly intrigued him, and leaning once more against his fir trees, he began to observe the stranger, a young man, fair-haired, who continued his work with ardor. What the devil is he "digging" for there? thought Alcide; has he found a gold mine? After a moment, the searcher stopped, then he seemed to examine an object he held in his hands. Five minutes later, he began to "poke" the ground again, and this time, apparently, he was filling in his hole. Good! thought the watcher, we'll go see this business up close, if he leaves. Indeed, he left, looking quite cheerful, and went back down the mountain by another path. Alcide, having waited a moment longer, went straight toward the mysterious hiding place. He easily discovered the freshly turned earth and, removing the stones, began in turn to dig. At a shallow depth, he laid his hand on a tin box which he picked up and found very light: "A bad sign," he said, "it's nothing very grand."

Without scruples, being as curious as an old maid, he opened the box, which contained a simple paper folded in four, resting on an orchid and a tuft of golden broom. He read these words on the note:

Happy is he who possesses a love,
A heart faithful upon his return.
In memory of August 28, 192*.
Zélie and Pierrot

The old bachelor was not long in understanding the story of the young lover coming here on a pilgrimage to revisit the places where, on a beautiful summer Sunday, facing the sparkling Alps, they had spent such sweet hours, happy moments of which they wanted the places themselves to keep the memory:
"...we have, in walking, left some trace,
Our heart has dreamed beneath the blue horizons."

Holding his unexpected find in his hands, our man found himself rather embarrassed at having thus penetrated the secret of this fresh idyll. But his bitterness as a suitor, long "pickled," resurfacing, he began to grumble:
"Yes, yes, all that is very fine, provided it lasts."

He even had a momentary temptation to write that on the paper, but for fear of being recognized, he put the object back in its place, covered it carefully, and, deep in thought, took the path back. And while descending, this phrase kept coming back to him: "A heart, a heart faithful upon your return." Not wanting for anything in the world to fall into what he called the foolishness of sentimentality, he inwardly gave himself a stern admonition, ending by saying aloud:
"Well, that serves you right, you old busybody; for once, you've been well caught; that will teach you not to stick your nose everywhere."

And considering this matter buried, he began to think about the morels that would surely be early this spring. He must not let his spots be stolen.

As for Zélie and Pierrot, if they went back to find their dear memories, they perhaps never suspected having thrown trouble for a moment into the heart of a good man. Fram.

de Bulgarie et de Grèce
Mgr. Stéphane, archevêque de Sofia,
rient d'adresser à l'Union internationale
de secours aux enfants une dépêche, où,
après avoir rendu hommage à cette
institution, il s'exprime comme suit :
La solidarité humaine ae manifeste le plue
sensiblement dane les heures critiques. Le
peuple bulgare est sincèrement reconnaissant
envers tous ceux qui, dans son épreuve
actuelle, lui ont témoigné sympathie et aide.
Dieu bénisse chaque effort qui soulagera la
souffrance, surtout celle des malheureux
petits.
D'autre part, l'U. I. S. E. reçoit de sa
déléguée la nouvelle qu'elle a pu assurer
une distribution quotidienne de pain à
3400 enfants dans les environs de
Philippopoli et, dans la ville même, de pain et
de thé à 2500 enfants. En outre, elle a
fourni des couvertures à l'hôpital de dix
baraques ouvert près de Philippopoli par
le chef de la garnison de cette ville, le
général Koutzeroff.
D'Athènes, le Dr Doxiadès, ancien
ministre, président de la Ligue patriotique
d'assistance aux enfants, télégraphie à
l'U. I. S. E. :
Envisageant le danger auquel sont exposés
les enfants de la population de Corinthe, la
Ligue patriotique fait appel aux généreux
sentiments de l'Union pour aider et faciliter
la bonne marche de l'œuvre de eecours
eutrperise.
Prière d'adresser tous dons à l'Union
internationale de secours aux enfants, 31
Quai du Mont-Blanc, Genève, ou à son
compte de chèques postaux I. 2051.

For the distressed children of Bulgaria and Greece

Monsignor Stéphane, Archbishop of Sofia, has sent a telegram to the International Union for Child Relief, in which, after paying tribute to this institution, he expresses himself as follows:

Human solidarity manifests itself most sensitively in critical times. The Bulgarian people are sincerely grateful to all those who, in their current ordeal, have shown them sympathy and aid. May God bless every effort that alleviates suffering, especially that of the unfortunate little ones.

On the other hand, the I.U.C.R. receives news from its delegate that she has been able to ensure a daily distribution of bread to 3,400 children in the vicinity of Philippopolis and, in the city itself, bread and tea to 2,500 children. Furthermore, she has supplied blankets to the ten-barrack hospital opened near Philippopolis by the commander of the city's garrison, General Koutzeroff.

From Athens, Dr. Doxiadès, former minister and president of the Patriotic League for Child Assistance, telegraphs the I.U.C.R.:

Considering the danger to which the children of the Corinthian population are exposed, the Patriotic League appeals to the generous sentiments of the Union to aid and facilitate the smooth progress of the relief work undertaken.

Please address all donations to the International Union for Child Relief, 31 Quai du Mont-Blanc, Geneva, or to its postal checking account I. 2051.

SPORTS
Cycling
THE 1949 TOUR DE FRANCE
(A.S.) — The organizers of the Tour de France have just resumed their work in preparation for the 1949 event. They will propose to the UCI calendar congress the period from July 7 to 31. However, the leaders of the Swiss Cycling Federation (SBB) would like the French organizers to move their event forward by one week so that a way can be found to insert the Tour de Switzerland between the Tour de France and the World Championships.
After exchanging views on the lessons from the 1948 race, the organizers decided that it would be run in the same direction, that is, from west to east. Many cities have submitted applications to the organizers, but the definitive itinerary will only be established later. The 1949 Tour will be contested under the formula of national and regional teams.

Football
VAST, FROM RACING PARIS,
SIGNS WITH SERVETTE
The Racing player Vast, now settled in Geneva, has sent his resignation letter to Racing and has signed with Servette. He will play next Sunday in Vevey with the team from the Parc des Sports.
Ben Barek, who is currently settled in Spain, is said to have already become a naturalized Spanish citizen. In this regard, it has been questioned whether he could play with the Spanish national team, but FIFA regulations do not allow a player who changes federations to defend the colors of a new country before a period of three years.

A CLASSIC MATCH
(A.S.) — To comply with a long-established tradition, a match was played on Wednesday at Highbury between the English champion Arsenal and the cup holder, Manchester United. This match generated a sum of £4,300, which was donated to a charity. 31,000 spectators attended the match, won by Arsenal 4-3.

Automobiles
AT THE PARIS MOTOR SHOW
(A.S.) — The International Motor Show was opened on Thursday in Paris. It will last until October 17. In total, there are about a hundred exhibitors: 82 manufacturers of passenger and utility vehicles and 58 coachbuilders presenting their products. There are also 9 exhibitors of bicycles and motorcycles.
The United States is represented by 19 companies, Great Britain by 14, Italy by 8, and Czechoslovakia by 3.
The International Automobile Federation will hold its congress during the Show and establish the international calendar.

COURTS EXTRAITS
Le carnet de bord des quatre bons
Helvètes, qui, soit dit en passant, ne
baragouinaient qu’à peine l’anglais,
est truffé de mots populaires
d’époque, du genre les pépées (pour les
filles), reluquer (les regarder) clapper
(manger), la turne (la chambre), en
écraser (dormir). A voir, nos gaillards
boivent pas mal (sauf au Pakistan...)
et fument autant. Le langage est
direct, sauf quand le thème impose un
développement. Quelques courts
ex-traits un peu au hasard.
A l’entrée en Bulgarie : « La douane se
passe fort bien, les douaniers nous
demandèrent juste si l’on avait des
montres : à notre réponse négative, ils
nous dirent que nous étions de
mauvais commerçants ».
Sur un bateau au large de Bahreïn :
« Les porteurs chargés comme des
mu-lets prennent la passerelle étroite
d’assaut, un vrai film de pirates à
l’abordage, et en même temps d’autres
porteurs redescendent par la même
échelle prendre livraison d’un
nouveau chargement, ce qui provoque des
embouteillages des familles (...).
Invités par une famille en Inde : « En
attendant le dîner, un des sikhs nous
apporte un gramophone à manivelle
et des disques hindous, et insiste au
moins une heure pour que « le Diable »
et « Simon » fassent une
démonstration de danse de chez nous.
Impossible de leur faire comprendre qu’en
Europe on danse avec une femme. »
Chez le médecin en Inde : « Il y a un
dispensaire, avec un toubib indigène,
genre charlatan, nous y amenons
« Scipion »; il fait une ordonnance en
hindou, la passe à son pharmacien
assis un peu plus loin entouré de
flacons de poudres de toutes les
couleurs (... )».

original_text: CONFEDERATION SUISSE (Corresp. particulière de la GAZETTE.) Neuchâtel, 23 septembre 1881 LA SOCIÉTÉ SUISSE D'UTILITÉ PUBLIQUE.Mes dépêches ont renseigné sommairement vos lecteurs sur les séances que la Société suisse d'utilité publique a tenues mercredi et jeudi à Neuchâtel.Laissez-moi compléter ces renseignements.Et. d'abord, il est un fait réjouissant, que la presse neuchâteloise a déjà constaté : c'est l'excellent esprit qui a animé les délibérations de la Société.Ou sentait véritablement vibrer dans tous les discours l'ardent amour du bien public, le désir de faire une œuvre utile au pays.On a été tenté quelquefois d'adresser à la Société d'utilité publique le reproche de se complaire dans l'étude théorique des questions, de se contenter d'émettre des vœux platoniques...Dans la séance de mercredi, on sentait au contraire la résolution bien arrêtée de ne pas se payer de mots, mais d'arriver à la possession d'un fait, à la réalisation de mesures pratiques.Et pourquoi cela ?— Confessons-le : Voire comme un Suisse est une locution qui mérite d'être proverbiale.Ainsi que l'a dit un orateur : Nous buvons trop !Non que nous soyons tous des ivrognes, loin de moi la pensée de traiter ainsi les autres et moi-même.Mais en Suisse — et c'est là peut-être un des dangers de notre vie démocratique, — on consomme infiniment plus de vin, de bière, d'alcool qu'il n'est utile ou nécessaire.M. Roulet, conseiller d'Etat, a cité a ce propos des chiffres qui devraient nous faire rougir.Les habitudes de café, la vie de cercle, la « soif électorale », comme on l'a nommée, nous font un tort incalculable : on boit sans soif, on dépense sans profit, et tel ouvrier, — c'est M. Sarasinqui l'a dit, — rapporte au bout de la semaine, à sa pauvre femme exténuée de travail, un franc sur vingt qu'il a gagnés.Cet ouvrier n'a pas eu besoin de se griser ; il a suffi de huvailler.Et quand je dis l'ouvrier, c'est un simple exemple.Si nous parlions des « messieurs », si nous parlions de nous-mêmes, n'aurions-nous pas des reproches analogues à nous adresser ?Les circonstances ne sont pas les mêmes ; mais les penchants se ressemblent étonnamment.Ce n'est pas à nous, Vaudois et Neuchâtelois, de le nier.En fin de compte, c'est la famille qui souffre de cette funeste habitude, devenue chez nûus si générale ; elle en est appauvrie et désorganisée.On a fini par comprendre en Suisse l'étendue du mal ; des hommes de cœur ont poussé le cri d'alarme.Il sera, je n'en puis douter, entendu dans la Suisse entière.Les mesures adoptées par l'Utilité publique sont les suivantes : L'ensemble de la question est renvoyé à une commission qui sera élue par la commission centrale et par le bureau de Neuchâtel.Cette commission entreprendra une véritable croisade contre l'alcoolisme et sera pourvue dans ce but d'un secrétaire rétribué, c'està dire qui consacrera son temps à cette eeuvre.La commission aura à compléter l'enquête encore insuffisante faite par MM.Roulet et Contesse, rapporteurs.Elle aura à étudier les divers moyens proposés.Parmi les remèdes recommandés par la Société, il faut mentionner celui que M. Schatzmann, de Lausanne, a proposé : provoquer l'élaboration d'une loi fédérale sur les auberges, qui sera une sorte de pendant à la loi sur les fabriques.Entre nous, je crois que cette loi n'est pas encore faite, et j'en suis à me demander si c'est là une loi désirable ; mais l'assemblée, emportée par un zèle méritoire, n'a guère hésité à émettre un vote favorable.L'école de l'abstinence a remporté aussi un succès.Je parle de ceux qui s'abstiennent afin de venir en aide à ceux auxquels l'usage modéré des boissons est devenu impossible.M. Rochat, président de la société de tempérance, a défendu avec une joyeuse éloquence. le système de privation héroïque auquel ses amis et lui se sont condamnés, et, après avoir entendu cet apôtre fervent, aussi large pour autrui que sévère pour lui-même, après avoir constaté que les abstinents ne songent point à étendre leur activité à tous leurs concitoyens ni à faire prévaloir leur système à l'exclusion de tout autre, bien des préventions se sont évanouies, et la Société a reconnu l'abstinence comme un moyen efficace et recommandable dans certains cas.Dorénavant, la question de l'ivrognerie et de l'abus des boissons est à l'ordre du jour en Suisse, et de la journée du 21 septembre sortiront, je le crois, des fruits bénis pour la patrie.Que la presse prenne à tâche et considère comme un honneur de seconder les efforts de la Société d'utilité publique !La presse fait trop souvent du mal pour ne pas saisir une occasion aussi favorable de faire le bien.C'est là un appel que j'adresse sérieusement à tous les journalistes mes confrères, car de l'énergie que nous déploierons dépend en quelque mesure le salut de notre peuple.La question de la protection de l'enfance malheureuse ou délaissée a fait aussi l'objet d'une longue discussion.Nous avons entendu l'avis d'hommes familiarisés avec cette importante question : MM.Guillaume, directeur de notre pénitencier, Ladame, directeur de notre orphelinat, Borel, Schneider, directeur de la Baîchtelen.C'est M. Lochmann, ce vénérable philanthrope que bien vous connaissez et auquel la colonie de Serix doit tant, qui a eu les honneurs de la discussion.Avec quelle autorité, et en même temps avec quelle bonhomie charmante, avec quelle familiarité mêlée de paternelle émotion il nous a raconté ses expériences et exposé son opinion sur l'ensemble du problème !Avec quelle bonne malice il a fait le procès à la charité officielle, à la charité de l'Etat, si sèche, si pauvre en somme et si dénuée d'entrailles !Comme il a bien esquissé le rôle de la charité individuelle et spontanée, libre de tous liens bureaucratiques et procédant non de la loi, mais de l'a-.Tant que notre pays possédera de tels hommes, l'utilité publique verra de beaux jours I La question a été renvoyée encore pour étude plus complète à la commission centrale.Si l'espace ne me faisait défaut, j'entrerais dans le détail des mesures proposées par les rapporteurs et des idées excellentes jetées dans le débat par M. Lecointe, de Genève, président du comité de Serix.Tout cela fera sans doute plus tard l'objet d'articles spéciaux.Les courses et les banquets qui ont suivi les séances ont été assaisonnés de cette gaîlé qui est la récompense du devoir accompli.Les gorges de l'Areuse, un bien joli site à recommander même aux habitants de votre incomparable canton de Vaud ; le château de Gorgier, une merveille d'antique architecture, appartenant au plus aimable des châtelains, M. Berthoud, de Londres ; le Devens, maison de travail et de correction pour les buveurs et les désœuvrés qui négligent leurs devoirs de famille, — voilà ce que nous avons eu de mieux à faire voir à nos confédérés.Ils ont paru y prendre plaisir.Dans le banquet d'hier, M. Numa Droz a fait un discours très applaudi sur les devises nationales (la vôtre a eu son petit paragraphe) et sur la grande devise suisse : Un pour tous, tous pour un ! que la Société d'utilité publique met si bien en pratique.Telle a été en gros cette fête, qui laisse à tous la meilleure impression.M. Aimé Humbert, ancien conseiller d'Etat, l'a bien dit dans un toast à la patrie : « Dès que » cette grande image de la patrie nous » apparaît, toutes les divisions sont ou-» bliées ; nous nous trouvons tous unis » dans un commun amour du bien pu-» blic.» C'est à Glaris que la Société tiendra l'an prochain ses assises.Qu'il nous soit donné de constater alors que les semences jetées hier en terre ont commencé à germer, pour le plus grand bonheur du peuple suisse !FRIBOURG.— Il y a quelque temps, en conduisant un bœuf à ferrer à Estavayer, il est arrivé une scène assez singulière.L'animal croyant peut-être qu'on le conduisait à la boucherie s'est échappé du côté de la porte de Grandcourt et s'est précipité du haut des falaises dans la grève du lac à une hauteur, nous assure-t-on, de 25 mètres sans éprouver le moindre mal.Après cette chute, à laquelle il n'était pas habitué du tout, l'animal est devenu furieux.On se proposait de le tuer à coups de fusil, lorsque cependant on est parvenu à le calmer et à l'arrêter.NEUCHATEL.— Un jeune homme a fait, samedi dernier, le trajet de Bâle à Neuchâtel en vélocipède.

SWISS CONFEDERATION (Special correspondence of the GAZETTE.) Neuchâtel, 23 September 1881

THE SWISS SOCIETY FOR PUBLIC UTILITY.

My dispatches have briefly informed your readers about the sessions that the Swiss Society for Public Utility held on Wednesday and Thursday in Neuchâtel. Allow me to complete this information.

And first, there is a heartening fact, already noted by the Neuchâtel press: it is the excellent spirit that animated the Society's deliberations. One truly felt vibrating in every speech an ardent love for the public good, the desire to do work useful for the country. The Society for Public Utility has sometimes been reproached for indulging in the theoretical study of questions, for being content to express platonic wishes... In Wednesday's session, one felt on the contrary a firm resolution not to be satisfied with words, but to achieve a concrete fact, the realization of practical measures.

And why is that?—Let us confess it: "Drink like a Swiss" is an expression that deserves to be proverbial. As one speaker said: We drink too much! Not that we are all drunkards—far be it from me to treat others and myself that way. But in Switzerland—and this is perhaps one of the dangers of our democratic life—infinitely more wine, beer, and alcohol is consumed than is useful or necessary. Mr. Roulet, State Councillor, cited figures on this point that should make us blush. Café habits, club life, "electoral thirst," as it has been called, cause us incalculable harm: we drink without thirst, we spend without profit, and such a worker—as Mr. Sarasinqui said—brings home to his poor wife, exhausted from work, one franc out of twenty that he earned. That worker did not need to get drunk; it was enough to "huvailler" [a play on words suggesting "to work" and "to drink"]. And when I say the worker, it is just an example. If we spoke of the "gentlemen," if we spoke of ourselves, would we not have similar reproaches to address to ourselves? The circumstances are not the same; but the inclinations are astonishingly similar. It is not for us, Vaudois and Neuchâtelois, to deny it. In the end, it is the family that suffers from this harmful habit, which has become so general among us; it is impoverished and disorganized by it.

People have finally come to understand the extent of the evil in Switzerland; men of heart have sounded the alarm. It will, I have no doubt, be heard throughout all of Switzerland. The measures adopted by the Public Utility Society are as follows: The whole question is referred to a commission which will be elected by the central commission and by the Neuchâtel bureau. This commission will undertake a veritable crusade against alcoholism and will be provided for this purpose with a paid secretary, that is, one who will devote his time to this work. The commission will have to complete the still insufficient inquiry made by Messrs. Roulet and Contesse, the reporters. It will have to study the various proposed means. Among the remedies recommended by the Society, one must mention that proposed by Mr. Schatzmann of Lausanne: to prompt the drafting of a federal law on inns, which will be a sort of counterpart to the factory law. Between us, I believe this law is not yet made, and I am left wondering if it is a desirable law; but the assembly, carried away by a praiseworthy zeal, hardly hesitated to cast a favorable vote.

The abstinence school also scored a success. I speak of those who abstain in order to help those for whom the moderate use of drinks has become impossible. Mr. Rochat, president of the temperance society, defended with joyful eloquence the system of heroic privation to which he and his friends have condemned themselves, and, after hearing this fervent apostle, as broad-minded for others as severe with himself, after noting that the abstainers do not at all think of extending their activity to all their fellow citizens nor of making their system prevail to the exclusion of all others, many prejudices vanished, and the Society recognized abstinence as an effective and commendable means in certain cases.

Henceforth, the question of drunkenness and the abuse of drinks is on the agenda in Switzerland, and from the day of 21 September will come, I believe, blessed fruits for the homeland. May the press take it upon itself and consider it an honor to support the efforts of the Society for Public Utility! The press too often does harm not to seize such a favorable opportunity to do good. This is an appeal I seriously address to all my fellow journalists, for the energy we deploy depends to some extent on the salvation of our people.

The question of the protection of unfortunate or abandoned children was also the subject of a long discussion. We heard the views of men familiar with this important question: Messrs. CONFEDERATION SUISSE (Corresp. particulière de la GAZETTE.) Neuchâtel, 23 septembre 1881 LA SOCIÉTÉ SUISSE D'UTILITÉ PUBLIQUE.Mes dépêches ont renseigné sommairement vos lecteurs sur les séances que la Société suisse d'utilité publique a tenues mercredi et jeudi à Neuchâtel.Laissez-moi compléter ces renseignements.Et. d'abord, il est un fait réjouissant, que la presse neuchâteloise a déjà constaté : c'est l'excellent esprit qui a animé les délibérations de la Société.Ou sentait véritablement vibrer dans tous les discours l'ardent amour du bien public, le désir de faire une œuvre utile au pays.On a été tenté quelquefois d'adresser à la Société d'utilité publique le reproche de se complaire dans l'étude théorique des questions, de se contenter d'émettre des vœux platoniques...Dans la séance de mercredi, on sentait au contraire la résolution bien arrêtée de ne pas se payer de mots, mais d'arriver à la possession d'un fait, à la réalisation de mesures pratiques.Et pourquoi cela ?— Confessons-le : Voire comme un Suisse est une locution qui mérite d'être proverbiale.Ainsi que l'a dit un orateur : Nous buvons trop !Non que nous soyons tous des ivrognes, loin de moi la pensée de traiter ainsi les autres et moi-même.Mais en Suisse — et c'est là peut-être un des dangers de notre vie démocratique, — on consomme infiniment plus de vin, de bière, d'alcool qu'il n'est utile ou nécessaire.M. Roulet, conseiller d'Etat, a cité a ce propos des chiffres qui devraient nous faire rougir.Les habitudes de café, la vie de cercle, la « soif électorale », comme on l'a nommée, nous font un tort incalculable : on boit sans soif, on dépense sans profit, et tel ouvrier, — c'est M. Sarasinqui l'a dit, — rapporte au bout de la semaine, à sa pauvre femme exténuée de travail, un franc sur vingt qu'il a gagnés.Cet ouvrier n'a pas eu besoin de se griser ; il a suffi de huvailler.Et quand je dis l'ouvrier, c'est un simple exemple.Si nous parlions des « messieurs », si nous parlions de nous-mêmes, n'aurions-nous pas des reproches analogues à nous adresser ?Les circonstances ne sont pas les mêmes ; mais les penchants se ressemblent étonnamment.Ce n'est pas à nous, Vaudois et Neuchâtelois, de le nier.En fin de compte, c'est la famille qui souffre de cette funeste habitude, devenue chez nûus si générale ; elle en est appauvrie et désorganisée.On a fini par comprendre en Suisse l'étendue du mal ; des hommes de cœur ont poussé le cri d'alarme.Il sera, je n'en puis douter, entendu dans la Suisse entière.Les mesures adoptées par l'Utilité publique sont les suivantes : L'ensemble de la question est renvoyé à une commission qui sera élue par la commission centrale et par le bureau de Neuchâtel.Cette commission entreprendra une véritable croisade contre l'alcoolisme et sera pourvue dans ce but d'un secrétaire rétribué, c'està dire qui consacrera son temps à cette eeuvre.La commission aura à compléter l'enquête encore insuffisante faite par MM.Roulet et Contesse, rapporteurs.Elle aura à étudier les divers moyens proposés.Parmi les remèdes recommandés par la Société, il faut mentionner celui que M. Schatzmann, de Lausanne, a proposé : provoquer l'élaboration d'une loi fédérale sur les auberges, qui sera une sorte de pendant à la loi sur les fabriques.Entre nous, je crois que cette loi n'est pas encore faite, et j'en suis à me demander si c'est là une loi désirable ; mais l'assemblée, emportée par un zèle méritoire, n'a guère hésité à émettre un vote favorable.L'école de l'abstinence a remporté aussi un succès.Je parle de ceux qui s'abstiennent afin de venir en aide à ceux auxquels l'usage modéré des boissons est devenu impossible.M. Rochat, président de la société de tempérance, a défendu avec une joyeuse éloquence. le système de privation héroïque auquel ses amis et lui se sont condamnés, et, après avoir entendu cet apôtre fervent, aussi large pour autrui que sévère pour lui-même, après avoir constaté que les abstinents ne songent point à étendre leur activité à tous leurs concitoyens ni à faire prévaloir leur système à l'exclusion de tout autre, bien des préventions se sont évanouies, et la Société a reconnu l'abstinence comme un moyen efficace et recommandable dans certains cas.Dorénavant, la question de l'ivrognerie et de l'abus des boissons est à l'ordre du jour en Suisse, et de la journée du 21 septembre sortiront, je le crois, des fruits bénis pour la patrie.Que la presse prenne à tâche et considère comme un honneur de seconder les efforts de la Société d'utilité publique !La presse fait trop souvent du mal pour ne pas saisir une occasion aussi favorable de faire le bien.C'est là un appel que j'adresse sérieusement à tous les journalistes mes confrères, car de l'énergie que nous déploierons dépend en quelque mesure le salut de notre peuple.La question de la protection de l'enfance malheureuse ou délaissée a fait aussi l'objet d'une longue discussion.Nous avons entendu l'avis d'hommes familiarisés avec cette importante question : MM.Guillaume, directeur de notre pénitencier, Ladame, directeur de notre orphelinat, Borel, Schneider, directeur de la Baîchtelen.C'est M. Lochmann, ce vénérable philanthrope que bien vous connaissez et auquel la colonie de Serix doit tant, qui a eu les honneurs de la discussion.Avec quelle autorité, et en même temps avec quelle bonhomie charmante, avec quelle familiarité mêlée de paternelle émotion il nous a raconté ses expériences et exposé son opinion sur l'ensemble du problème !Avec quelle bonne malice il a fait le procès à la charité officielle, à la charité de l'Etat, si sèche, si pauvre en somme et si dénuée d'entrailles !Comme il a bien esquissé le rôle de la charité individuelle et spontanée, libre de tous liens bureaucratiques et procédant non de la loi, mais de l'a-.Tant que notre pays possédera de tels hommes, l'utilité publique verra de beaux jours I La question a été renvoyée encore pour étude plus complète à la commission centrale.Si l'espace ne me faisait défaut, j'entrerais dans le détail des mesures proposées par les rapporteurs et des idées excellentes jetées dans le débat par M. Lecointe, de Genève, président du comité de Serix.Tout cela fera sans doute plus tard l'objet d'articles spéciaux.Les courses et les banquets qui ont suivi les séances ont été assaisonnés de cette gaîlé qui est la récompense du devoir accompli.Les gorges de l'Areuse, un bien joli site à recommander même aux habitants de votre incomparable canton de Vaud ; le château de Gorgier, une merveille d'antique architecture, appartenant au plus aimable des châtelains, M. Berthoud, de Londres ; le Devens, maison de travail et de correction pour les buveurs et les désœuvrés qui négligent leurs devoirs de famille, — voilà ce que nous avons eu de mieux à faire voir à nos confédérés.Ils ont paru y prendre plaisir.Dans le banquet d'hier, M. Numa Droz a fait un discours très applaudi sur les devises nationales (la vôtre a eu son petit paragraphe) et sur la grande devise suisse : Un pour tous, tous pour un ! que la Société d'utilité publique met si bien en pratique.Telle a été en gros cette fête, qui laisse à tous la meilleure impression.M. Aimé Humbert, ancien conseiller d'Etat, l'a bien dit dans un toast à la patrie : « Dès que » cette grande image de la patrie nous » apparaît, toutes les divisions sont ou-» bliées ; nous nous trouvons tous unis » dans un commun amour du bien pu-» blic.» C'est à Glaris que la Société tiendra l'an prochain ses assises.Qu'il nous soit donné de constater alors que les semences jetées hier en terre ont commencé à germer, pour le plus grand bonheur du peuple suisse !FRIBOURG.— Il y a quelque temps, en conduisant un bœuf à ferrer à Estavayer, il est arrivé une scène assez singulière.L'animal croyant peut-être qu'on le conduisait à la boucherie s'est échappé du côté de la porte de Grandcourt et s'est précipité du haut des falaises dans la grève du lac à une hauteur, nous assure-t-on, de 25 mètres sans éprouver le moindre mal.Après cette chute, à laquelle il n'était pas habitué du tout, l'animal est devenu furieux.On se proposait de le tuer à coups de fusil, lorsque cependant on est parvenu à le calmer et à l'arrêter.NEUCHATEL.— Un jeune homme a fait, samedi dernier, le trajet de Bâle à Neuchâtel en vélocipède.

SWISS CONFEDERATION (Special correspondence of the GAZETTE.) Neuchâtel, 23 September 1881

THE SWISS SOCIETY FOR PUBLIC UTILITY.

My dispatches have briefly informed your readers about the sessions that the Swiss Society for Public Utility held on Wednesday and Thursday in Neuchâtel. Allow me to complete this information.

And first, there is a heartening fact, already noted by the Neuchâtel press: it is the excellent spirit that animated the Society's deliberations. One truly felt vibrating in every speech an ardent love for the public good, the desire to do work useful for the country. The Society for Public Utility has sometimes been reproached for indulging in the theoretical study of questions, for being content to express platonic wishes... In Wednesday's session, one felt on the contrary a firm resolution not to be satisfied with words, but to achieve a concrete fact, the realization of practical measures.

And why is that?—Let us confess it: "Drink like a Swiss" is an expression that deserves to be proverbial. As one speaker said: We drink too much! Not that we are all drunkards—far be it from me to treat others and myself that way. But in Switzerland—and this is perhaps one of the dangers of our democratic life—infinitely more wine, beer, and alcohol is consumed than is useful or necessary. Mr. Roulet, State Councillor, cited figures on this point that should make us blush. Café habits, club life, "electoral thirst," as it has been called, cause us incalculable harm: we drink without thirst, we spend without profit, and such a worker—as Mr. Sarasinqui said—brings home to his poor wife, exhausted from work, one franc out of twenty that he earned. That worker did not need to get drunk; it was enough to "huvailler" [a play on words suggesting "to work" and "to drink"]. And when I say the worker, it is just an example. If we spoke of the "gentlemen," if we spoke of ourselves, would we not have similar reproaches to address to ourselves? The circumstances are not the same; but the inclinations are astonishingly similar. It is not for us, Vaudois and Neuchâtelois, to deny it. In the end, it is the family that suffers from this harmful habit, which has become so general among us; it is impoverished and disorganized by it.

People have finally come to understand the extent of the evil in Switzerland; men of heart have sounded the alarm. It will, I have no doubt, be heard throughout all of Switzerland. The measures adopted by the Public Utility Society are as follows: The whole question is referred to a commission which will be elected by the central commission and by the Neuchâtel bureau. This commission will undertake a veritable crusade against alcoholism and will be provided for this purpose with a paid secretary, that is, one who will devote his time to this work. The commission will have to complete the still insufficient inquiry made by Messrs. Roulet and Contesse, the reporters. It will have to study the various proposed means. Among the remedies recommended by the Society, one must mention that proposed by Mr. Schatzmann of Lausanne: to prompt the drafting of a federal law on inns, which will be a sort of counterpart to the factory law. Between us, I believe this law is not yet made, and I am left wondering if it is a desirable law; but the assembly, carried away by a praiseworthy zeal, hardly hesitated to cast a favorable vote.

The abstinence school also scored a success. I speak of those who abstain in order to help those for whom the moderate use of drinks has become impossible. Mr. Rochat, president of the temperance society, defended with joyful eloquence the system of heroic privation to which he and his friends have condemned themselves, and, after hearing this fervent apostle, as broad-minded for others as severe with himself, after noting that the abstainers do not at all think of extending their activity to all their fellow citizens nor of making their system prevail to the exclusion of all others, many prejudices vanished, and the Society recognized abstinence as an effective and commendable means in certain cases.

Henceforth, the question of drunkenness and the abuse of drinks is on the agenda in Switzerland, and from the day of 21 September will come, I believe, blessed fruits for the homeland. May the press take it upon itself and consider it an honor to support the efforts of the Society for Public Utility! The press too often does harm not to seize such a favorable opportunity to do good. This is an appeal I seriously address to all my fellow journalists, for the energy we deploy depends to some extent on the salvation of our people.

The question of the protection of unfortunate or abandoned children was also the subject of a long discussion. We heard the views of men familiar with this important question: Messrs. Guillaume, director of our penitentiary; Ladame, director of our orphanage; Borel; Schneider, director of Baîchtelen. It was Mr. Lochmann, that venerable philanthropist whom you know well and to whom the Serix colony owes so much, who had the honors of the discussion. With what authority, and at the same time with what charming good nature, with what familiarity mixed with paternal emotion he told us of his experiences and expounded his opinion on the whole problem! With what good-natured mischief he prosecuted official charity, state charity, so dry, so poor in sum and so devoid of heart! How well he outlined the role of individual and spontaneous charity, free from all bureaucratic ties and proceeding not from the law, but from the heart! As long as our country possesses such men, public utility will see fine days! The question was again referred for more complete study to the central commission.

If space did not fail me, I would go into the details of the measures proposed by the reporters and the excellent ideas thrown into the debate by Mr. Lecointe of Geneva, president of the Serix committee. All this will no doubt later be the subject of special articles.

The outings and banquets that followed the sessions were seasoned with that gaiety which is the reward of duty accomplished. The gorges of the Areuse, a very pretty site to recommend even to the inhabitants of your incomparable canton of Vaud; the castle of Gorgier, a marvel of ancient architecture, belonging to the most amiable of castle owners, Mr. Berthoud of London; the Devens, a work and correction house for drinkers and idlers who neglect their family duties—that is what we had best to show our confederates. They seemed to take pleasure in it.

At yesterday's banquet, Mr. Numa Droz gave a much-applauded speech on national mottos (yours had its little paragraph) and on the great Swiss motto: "One for all, all for one!" which the Society for Public Utility puts into practice so well.

Mr. Aimé Humbert, former State Councillor, said it well in a toast to the homeland: "As soon as this great image of the homeland appears to us, all divisions are forgotten; we find ourselves all united in a common love of the public good." AFFRIQUE. — Algiers, 10 July. FOREIGN NEWS. An English frigate has just anchored in this port. It performed the customary salute; it carried an agent of Admiral Nelson. This is the third humiliating step the English have taken with the Dey. In the first, Nelson came to anchor before Algiers with 17 ships of the line and a proportionate number of frigates; he made great threats to obtain the reinstatement of the English agent, expelled some months earlier; the restitution of confiscated ships, the freedom of the crews, and of English, Maltese, and Neapolitan slaves; compensation for the losses that the Algerian navy had inflicted on the English; finally, apologies from the Dey for the treatment that British agents and subjects had endured. The Dey refused everything and responded only with a lit fuse.

A month later, a negotiation took place. The English consented to their agent not returning to Algiers and demanded the freedom of English, Maltese, and Neapolitan slaves. They obtained only a refusal.

The frigate that has just anchored most recently limited its demands further and now sought only provisions and the freedom of English slaves. It was again refused. The Dey demands 180,000 piastres in compensation for a cargo seized three years ago; he does not wish to receive the former English agent and demands another. Thus, the English demand in vain apologies, compensation, the freedom of slaves, etc.; and it is the Dey who lays down the law. Since Algiers has existed, not even the smallest powers of Europe have submitted to such dishonorable steps.

completion: ENGLAND, LONDON, July 22. English newspapers continue to speculate on the actions of the former and future ministries, without providing any definitive information on this matter. Meanwhile, the main leaders of the party are publishing their manifestos. Among these, the one by Lord John Russell stands out, addressed by this minister to the voters of the City, on the eve of his marriage to Lady Fanny Elliott. In this document, Lord John Russell acknowledges without hesitation the defeat of his party. He then outlines the course that the Whig ministry intends to follow in the circumstances created by the recent elections. "The result of the appeal we will make to Parliament," he says, "can easily be foreseen... And as no ministers of the Crown can maintain themselves without the confidence of the House of Commons, our withdrawal from power will immediately follow the condemnation of our policy." The ministry can therefore be considered dissolved; however, it is believed that it will still present itself before the new Parliament, and no one here doubts that the young Queen herself will wish to open the new session, as she wished to close the last one. If the ministers remain in power, it is because it is customary in England for a ministry to resign only following a vote of the chambers, but Lord John Russell's letter is itself an act of resignation. It is also a program of opposition, and it is in this capacity that it deserves the most attention. Lord Russell continues in this vein. "As soon as," he says, "the new Parliament is assembled, we will seize the first opportunity to request a clear and decisive judgment on the measures we have proposed." Thus, one should expect a parliamentary struggle to be engaged in all its forms over the address. The speech from the throne will undoubtedly praise the measures requested by the Whigs. The opposition will propose a condemnatory amendment; then the vote will come, and if the majority declares against the ministry, it will resign. The ministers cannot decently follow any other course. The Sun announces a list of members of the Tory cabinet, different from the one previously published. The essential change noted there is the appointment, as Prime Minister, of Lord Aberdeen in place of Sir Robert Peel. The notable reluctance that has manifested itself in high places against Sir Robert Peel makes this change very probable. The Tories and Sir Robert Peel in particular are said to be inclined to accept this plan as a means of regaining the Queen's favor.

original_text: Proche-Orient : jeux avec le feu Pourquoi Syriens et Israéliens menacent-ils soudain de s'affronter dans une guerre risquant d'embraser tout le Proche-Orient ?L'explication immédiate est connue : pour aider leurs « protégés » chrétiens de la vallée libanaise de la Bekaa, pilonnés par les Syriens, les Israéliens ont fait donner leur aviation et, au cours d'un raid, le 28 avril dernier, abattu deux hélicoptères damascènes.La Syrie a réagi instantanément, installant au Liban quelque 14 batteries de missiles sol-air SAM.Israël, estimant que cette implantation mettait en cause la suprématie aérienne dont il bénéficiait depuis plusieurs années au Liban, et bouleversait du coup, en sa défaveur, le délicat équilibre régional, exigea de Damas qu'il retire ses missiles.Devant le refus syrien, Israël décidait, de l'aveu même du premier ministre Begin, de détruire ces batteries de missiles, le 30 avril dernier, mais y renonça momentanément pour des raisons météorologiques, puis indéfiniment, à la demande instante du général Alexander Haig.Cette explication est cependant insuffisante.Si Israéliens et Syriens voulaient éviter de s'affronter militairement, il leur serait facile de trouver un compromis.Alors, en entretenant la tension entre eux, qu'essaient-ils de dire, et à qui ?La réponse est évidente : les deux capitales tentent désespéramment d'éveiller l'intérêt des Etats-Unis, et d'attirer ces derniers dans leur jeu respectif.Sur le mode : « Faites quelque chose, arrêteznous, ou nous ne répondons plus de rien ».Depuis l'élection de Ronald Reagan, les Américains ont montré les dispositions suivantes à l'égard du Proche-Orient : 1) priorité générale à la lutte contre l'expansionnisme soviétique ; 2) priorité régionale aux problèmes du Golfe (sécurité des approvisionnements pétroliers ); et 3) volonté de mobiliser des ressources considérables pour atteindre ces objectifs._ Or, jadis, le conflit israélo-arabe était au centre de toute stratégie procheorientale : les protagonistes du conflit en ont tiré, de longues années durant, d'énormes avantages financiers, militaires et politiques.On comprend que l'idée de retomber dans l'ombre, l'oubli, l'indifférence, leur apparaisse aujourd'hui insupportable.A travers une menace de guerre que les Etats-Unis sont appelés à régler comme médiateurs, dans une atmosphère de tension sans cesse changeante, sinusoïdale intensément dramatique, Us ont le sûr instinct de pouvoir retrouver un poids qu'ils étaient en train de perdre.Le raisonnement est particulièrement vrai pour Israël qui a vu, il y a quelques semaines, les Etats-Unis disposés à vendre des radars volants à l'Arabie Saoudite, dans un souci prioritaire de renforcer un front antisoviétique dans la région, et en négligeant de considérer les craintes que cette transaction ne pouvait manquer d'éveiller à Jérusalem.La Syrie, quant à elle, a fait savoir à Philip Habib, le médiateur dépêché par Ronald Reagan, que les Etats-Unis étaient seuls à pouvoir influencer efficacement la politique israélienne.Une manière de leur dire : « Voudriez-vous vraiment que nous fussions obligés d'appeler l'URSS à notre aide ?» A ce stade, on peut dire que les Américains se sont laissés prendre au piège.Cela parce qu'ils sont pleins d'une énergie qui cherche emploi, mais n'ont pas encore de politiques spécifiques, ce qui les rend faciles à manœuvrer.L'Amérique roulée dans un bazar oriental !Le risque n'est pas négligeable cependant que les acteurs, qui feignent de vouloir s'entr'égorger, se prennent à leur propre jeu, et que le jeu tourne au massacre.

The Middle East: Playing with Fire
Why are Syrians and Israelis suddenly threatening to confront each other in a war that risks engulfing the entire Middle East?
The immediate explanation is known: to aid their "protected" Christians in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, who were being shelled by the Syrians, the Israelis deployed their air force and, during a raid on April 28, shot down two Syrian helicopters.
Syria reacted instantly, installing around 14 surface-to-air missile batteries in Lebanon.
Israel, believing that this deployment challenged the air supremacy it had enjoyed for several years in Lebanon and upset the delicate regional balance against its favor, demanded that Damascus withdraw its missiles.
Following Syria's refusal, Israel decided, as Prime Minister Begin himself admitted, to destroy these missile batteries on April 30, but temporarily abandoned the plan due to weather conditions, and then indefinitely, at the urgent request of General Alexander Haig.
This explanation, however, is insufficient.
If Israelis and Syrians wanted to avoid military confrontation, they could easily find a compromise.
So, by maintaining tension between them, what are they trying to say, and to whom?
The answer is obvious: both capitals are desperately trying to awaken the interest of the United States and draw them into their respective games.
In the manner of: "Do something, stop us, or we won't be responsible for anything."
Since Ronald Reagan's election, Americans have shown the following dispositions regarding the Middle East: 1) general priority to combating Soviet expansionism; 2) regional priority to Gulf problems (security of oil supplies); and 3) willingness to mobilize considerable resources to achieve these objectives.
Yet, formerly, the Israeli-Arab conflict was at the center of any Middle Eastern strategy: the protagonists of the conflict derived enormous financial, military, and political advantages from it for many years.
It is understandable that the idea of falling back into shadow, oblivion, indifference now seems unbearable to them.
Through a threat of war that the United States is called to mediate, in an atmosphere of constantly changing, intensely dramatic sinusoidal tension, they have the sure instinct of regaining a weight they were losing.
This reasoning is particularly true for Israel, which saw, a few weeks ago, the United States willing to sell airborne radars to Saudi Arabia, prioritizing the reinforcement of an anti-Soviet front in the region, and neglecting to consider the fears this transaction inevitably aroused in Jerusalem.
Syria, meanwhile, informed Philip Habib, the mediator dispatched by Ronald Reagan, that the United States alone could effectively influence Israeli policy.
A way of telling them: "Would you really want us to be forced to call on the USSR for help?"
At this stage, it can be said that Americans have fallen into the trap.
This is because they are full of energy seeking employment but have no specific policies yet, making them easy to maneuver.
America rolled in an oriental bazaar!
The risk, however, is not negligible that the actors, who pretend to want to slaughter each other, become caught in their own game, and the game turns into a massacre.

figurons encore, malgré tous nos péchés
politiques !) par un arrêt de l'Olympe pour être
rejetés dans les rangs de la majorité à laquelle
seule on applique le principe : Une seule et
même justice pour tous. J. B. RUSCH.

completion:
Letter from the German Swiss
(We will be pleased to publish from time to time, under this heading, articles by the good Swiss that is Mr. J.-B. Rusch, who has kindly agreed to collaborate with us.)

Neuenhof, near Wettingen,
April 19, 1918.

When, one day, one of my schoolmates had to give the definition of the word "history," he replied without thinking for long: "History is a chronicle of affairs." The class then made great fun of him, and from that day on, my poor friend was stuck with the nickname "Chronicle of Affairs."

But now that I belong, in the land of the Helvetians, to that privileged category of press people, now that I have known for many years what politics is, I no longer laugh at that definition. At least when, speaking of Swiss history, one thinks of contemporary history under the regime of emergency powers, of that Helvetian Cleopatra. Here, the insipid answer of an unconscious schoolboy finds its confirmation in the political life of a state, which is not exactly proof of the capability of its leaders.

The history of Switzerland under the emergency powers regime is indeed a "chronicle of affairs," and in the future, the best way to safeguard the political reputation of a few magistrates, their collaborators, and subordinates will be the complete forgetting of their deeds. But, however convenient this forgetting may be for many people, it would nevertheless lack, to be considered a virtue, the utilitarian effect.

One of the many "affairs" that we have experienced and that we are already beginning to forget is the "Schœller Affair." Who among us does not remember that upright man who had millions transported under the protection of a neutral diplomatic suitcase? There were many people who were extremely angry with this friend of our venerable general for not having been clever enough to avoid the most unfortunate fate that can befall a private individual from a neutral country who abuses his diplomatic mail: namely, getting caught, if not in the act, then at least shortly afterward, thanks to the good memory of a simple Parisian taxi driver!

It is not for us to judge whether this poor opinion of the Swiss people is justified or not, since we belong to that happy category of citizens of the republic who do not know everything. But what struck us particularly and what should have awakened in all of us who love cleanliness in the house is that the Federal Council reprimanded Mr. Schœller by expressing its disapproval. This gesture, the Federal Council had no right to make. Mr. Schœller is not a federal official, but a mere private individual.

If the Federal Council had been of the opinion that the Schœller affair was an act tarnishing Swiss neutrality, whose virginal reputation we wish to safeguard for family reasons, it would have been its duty—and it still is at this hour—to order an investigation! Either Mr. Schœller is guilty, then he is to be judged like any other mortal who does not have the luck, like him, to be able to rely on family protections and friends in such high places. Or he is innocent, then what is the point of this comedy of a reprimand from the executive power? We are far from envying Mr. Schœller the tranquility with which he accepts a reprimand from an authority that has neither to praise nor to blame, but which is solely instituted to govern and to oversee! To establish his innocence in the eyes of public opinion, which is following this affair closely, Mr. Schœller should have demanded an investigation after the Federal Council's reprimand. He did nothing of the sort, which is why we are doing it today for him, hoping, however, that in doing so we will not be too disagreeable to him.

It is certain that if a French-speaking Swiss citizen had found himself in the same unfortunate situation as Mr. Schœller, an official investigation would have been demanded. We therefore demand it today for Mr. Schœller, either for his justification or for his indictment!

In case of rehabilitation, the Federal Council owes him satisfaction for the reprimand; if he is guilty of criminal acts, he must be condemned and not reprimanded!

We do not wish that, alongside so many other abuses, a difference should persist between a majority of Swiss who are brought to trial and a minority who are simply reprimanded by the executive power.

We must proclaim this aloud, even at the risk of exposing ourselves through this demand to expulsion from the bosom of this minority of demigods (among whom we still figure, despite all our political sins!) by a decree of Olympus, to be cast back into the ranks of the majority to which alone the principle is applied: One and the same justice for all. J. B. RUSCH.

SUISSE
Un nouveau danger. — On mande de Berne
à la < Gazette de Lausanne > :
La démocratie suisse est sortie à son
honneur d'une crise redoutable. Rien ne serait plus
dangereux et plus trompeur que de s'imaginer
que, du jour au lendemain, nous allons voir
notre pays rentrer dans le calme et la
tranquillité. A peine avons-nous eu le temps de nous
réjouir du rétablissement de l'ordre que de
nouveaux et plus graves dangers nous menacent
D'après des renseignements sûrs qui viennent
de parvenir au Conseil fédéral, les armées
_aOemandes refluent vers l'intérieur dans un
désordre et une anarchie plus grandes encore que
les armées autrichiennes après la cessation
brusque des hostilités. Ces millions d'hommes
trouvent leur pays en pleine décomposition :
partout les autorités régulîères sont
remplacées par des conseils d'ouvriers et de soldats.
Les officiers sont entièrement débordés, toute
autorité militaire et civile a disparu. La

SWITZERLAND
A new danger. — The Gazette de Lausanne reports from Bern:

Swiss democracy has emerged with honor from a formidable crisis. Nothing would be more dangerous and deceptive than to imagine that, overnight, we will see our country return to calm and tranquility. We have barely had time to rejoice at the restoration of order when new and more serious dangers threaten us.

According to reliable information that has just reached the Federal Council, the German armies are retreating inland in even greater disorder and anarchy than the Austrian armies after the abrupt cessation of hostilities. These millions of men find their country in complete disintegration: everywhere the regular authorities are being replaced by workers' and soldiers' councils. Officers are completely overwhelmed; all military and civil authority has vanished. The turmoil of minds is terrifying.

These events affect us directly in that masses of soldiers are trying to cross into Switzerland. These are precisely the most dangerous and fanatical elements. In the general confusion, passports are no longer an issue. The men want to cross into Switzerland, willingly or by force, drawn by a very powerful current. The main thing for them is to cross the border by any means, and the workers' and soldiers' councils, far from suppressing this movement, are doing everything in their power to encourage it. These disbanded armies have enthusiastically welcomed the news of the general strike in Switzerland.

The number of those who want to enter our country is estimated at around 80,000.

It goes without saying that we cannot receive them under the conditions in which they present themselves and given the sentiments they express. We have not emerged from the general strike only to fall into even more formidable dangers, if that is possible.

The Federal Council will be obliged to take special measures to protect our country from this invasion, which is anything but peaceful. The events of recent days have shown that our people are firmly resolved to prevent order from being disturbed in our land, in any manner whatsoever. There is no doubt, unfortunately, that the news of this new danger will be welcomed with joy by the organizers of the general strike, who, by all means at their disposal—and they are numerous, varied, and insidious—will seek to exploit this movement to achieve their ends and avenge their failure.

The civic union that instantly formed around the Federal Council and the regular authorities when the hour of danger struck will manifest with the same strength in this new peril. This is all the more indispensable because, in addition to the external front formed by the troops guarding the Rhine border, we will be obliged to establish an internal front against all elements of social disintegration at work within our country.

Diplomatic corps. — Professor Förster has just been appointed, provisionally, as minister of the new Bavarian People's State to the Swiss Confederation.

Having taught for many years at the Federal Polytechnic School and the University of Zurich, Mr. Förster is a faithful friend of our country and knows it well.

Swiss Federal Railways (CFF). — It is learned that the general management of the Swiss Federal Railways has ordered that no storage fees be charged for goods that remained in stations beyond the regulatory deadlines due to the general strike; nor will any delay penalties be charged for wagons that could not be loaded or unloaded in time for the same reason.

Inquiries. — The Federal Council has opened an inquiry into the Bolshevik movement in Switzerland. The Attorney General of the Confederation and the federal examining magistrates are tasked with conducting this inquiry.

The Federal Council has issued special instructions for the judicial inquiry that must identify all those guilty of unlawful acts during the strike.

Grimm and Platten to be prosecuted. — The Federal Council has decided to prosecute Grimm and Platten for organizing a Bolshevik movement in Switzerland.

The cost of the general strike. — The Bund estimates that the losses of all kinds and the expenses due to the three-day general strike amount to between 25 and 30 million francs.

Lausanne Civic Union. — On Saturday evening, at the Montbenon casino, in a very fine and vibrant assembly attended by numerous citizens, the Lausanne Civic Union was established.

Regarding the German consulate in Zurich. — The Gazette de Lausanne learns from Zurich, from a reliable source, that three Germans employed at the German general consulate played an active role in directing the strike.

An irreconcilable. — The Mülhauser Tagblatt reports that Admiral Tirpitz, the promoter of unrestricted submarine warfare, has recently sold his villa in Haslach (Grand Duchy of Baden) and has traveled to Switzerland incognito.

Serious fire. — A fire broke out on Saturday afternoon in the airship hangar at the Bern drill ground. Several captive balloons were seriously damaged.

BERN. — As was the case in Zurich, numerous cases of influenza are reported among the occupation troops mobilized in Bern. A large number of patients are being cared for in the barracks, where volunteer nurses have made themselves available to the military authorities. Among the patients is the commander of the Fribourg regiment, Colonel de Diesbach. The 16th Fribourg battalion left the federal capital on Friday, cheered by the public.

SOLOTHURN. — During the strike incidents in Solothurn and Grenchen, 23 people were arrested. These arrests have been upheld.

The editor of the Freie Zeitung and municipal councilor Simond Braunschweig of Solothurn have fled.

BASEL-CITY. — The Grand Council discussed interpellations regarding the strike. Several speakers demanded that the bourgeois members of the State Council face the consequences of their conciliatory attitude toward the strikers.
