SUISSE
Un nouveau danger. — On mande de Berne
à la < Gazette de Lausanne > :
La démocratie suisse est sortie à son
honneur d'une crise redoutable. Rien ne serait plus
dangereux et plus trompeur que de s'imaginer
que, du jour au lendemain, nous allons voir
notre pays rentrer dans le calme et la
tranquillité. A peine avons-nous eu le temps de nous
réjouir du rétablissement de l'ordre que de
nouveaux et plus graves dangers nous menacent
D'après des renseignements sûrs qui viennent
de parvenir au Conseil fédéral, les armées
_aOemandes refluent vers l'intérieur dans un
désordre et une anarchie plus grandes encore que
les armées autrichiennes après la cessation
brusque des hostilités. Ces millions d'hommes
trouvent leur pays en pleine décomposition :
partout les autorités régulîères sont
remplacées par des conseils d'ouvriers et de soldats.
Les officiers sont entièrement débordés, toute
autorité militaire et civile a disparu. La
perturbation des esprits est effravante.
Ces événements nous touchent directement
en ce que des masses de soldats cherchent à
passer en Suisse. Ce sout précisément les
éléments les plus dangereux et les plus exaltés.
Dans la confusion générale, il n'est plus
question de passeports. Les hommes veulent passer
de gré ou de force en Suisse, vers laqueUe ils
sont portés par un courant très puissant Le
principal pour eux est de franchir la frontière
par n'importe quel moyen et les conseils d'
ouvriers et de soldats, loin de réprimer ce
mouvement font tout ce qui est en leur pouvoir pour
le favoriser. Ces armées débandées ont
accueilli avec enthousiasme la nouvelle de la crève
céiérale en Suisse.
On évalue à 80,000 environ le nombre de
ceux qui veulent pénétrer chez nous.
Il va de soi que nous ne saurions les
recevoir dans les conditions où ils se présentent et
étant donné les sentiments qu'ils manifestent.
Nous ne sommes pas sortis de la grève
générale pour retomber dans des dangers plus
redoutables encore, s'il est possible.
Le Conseil fédéral sera obligé de prendre
des mesures spéciales pour préserver notre
pays de cet envahissement, qui n'a rien de
cifique. Les événements de ces derniers jours
ont montré que notre peuple est fermement
résolu à empêcher que l'ordre ne soit troublé
chez nous, de quelque manière que ce soit. Il
n'est pas douteux, malheureusement, que la
nouvelle de ce nouveau danger ne soit
accueillie avec joie par les organisateurs de la grève
générale qui, par tous les moyens dont ils
disposent — ils sont nombreux, variés et
perfides — chercheront à exploiter ce mouvement
pour arriver à leurs fins et se venger de leur
échec.
L'union civique qui s'est instantanément
formée autour du Conseil fédéral et des autorités
régulières lorsqu'à sonné l'heure du danger se
manifestera avec la même force dans ce
nouveau péril. C'est d'autant plus indispensable
qu'au front extérieur que forment les troupes
qui veillent aux bords du Rhin, nous serons
obligés d'ajouter un front intérieur contre tous
les éléments do décomposition sociale oui
travaillent chez nous.
Corps diplomatique. — Le pi-oîesseur Fôrster
vient d'être nommé, à titre provisoire, ministre
du nouvel Etat populaire bavarois auprès de la
Confédération suisse. ¦
Ayant enseigné durant de longues années à
l'Ecole polytechnique fédérale et à l'Université
de Zurich, M. Fôrster est un fidèle ami de notre
pays et le connaît de près.
C. F. F. — On apprend que la direction
générale des C. F. F. a donné l'ordre de ne pas percevoir
de frais de magasinage pour les marchandises
qui ont séjourné dans les gares au-delà des
délais réglementaires par suite de la grève
générale ; il ne sera pas non plus perçu d'indemnités
de retard pour les vagons qui n'ont pas pu être
chargés ou déchargés en temps utile pour le
même motif.
Enquêtes. —• Le Conseil fédéral a ouvert une
enquête sur le mouvement bolchevik en Suisse.
Le procureur général de la Confédération et
les juges d'instruction fédéraux sont chargés
de mener ceite enquête.
Le Conseil fédéral a décrété des instructions
spéciales en vue de l'enquête judiciaire qui doit
rechercher tous ceux qui se sont rendus
coupables d'actes illicites pendant la grève.
Grimm ot FÏatten seront poursuivis. —Lo
Conseil fédéral a décidé de poursuivie Grimm
et Platten pour avoir organisé cil Suisse un
mouvement _bolchôviste.
Le bilan (le la grève générale.-— Le « Bund »
calcule que les pertes de lout genre et les
_dépenses dues aux trois-jours de grève générale
s'élèvent de'_^ 5 à 30 millions de trancs.
Union civique lausannoise. — Samedi soir,
au casino de Montbenon, dans nne très belle et
très vibrante assemblée, n laquelle assistaient de
nombreux citoyens, a été constituée l'Union
civique lausannoiso.
_Euroro le _consulat allemand do Zurich .- —
La « Gazette de Lausanne » apprend de Zurich,
de source sûre, quo trois Allemands employés au
consulat général d'Allemagne, ont joué un rôle
actif dans la direction de la grève.
Un radesirsible. — Lo « Mûhlhauser Tagblau >
annonce que l'amiral Tiçpitz, le promoteur de la,
_guerro sous-marinc à outrance, a vendu, ces
jours-ci, sa villa de Haslach (duché de Bade) et,
qu'il s'est rendu en Suisse incognito.
Grave incendie. — Un incendie a éclaté
samedi après midi dans le hangar d'aêrcstats de la
place d'exercices de berne. Plusieurs ballons
captifs ont été gravement endommagés.
BERNE. — Ainsi que cela s'est produit à
Zurich, de nombreux cas de grippe sont signalés
parmi les troupes d'occupation mobilisées à
Berne. Un grand nombre de malades sont soignés à
la caserne, où des infirmiers volontaires se sont
mis à la disposition de l'autorité militaire.
Parmi les malades se trouve le commandant du
régiment fribourgeois, le colonel de Diesbach.
Le bataillon fribourgeois 16 a quitté vendredi la
ville fédérale, acclamé par le public.
SOLEURE. — Au cours des incidents de grève
à Soleure et à Granges, 23 personnes ont été
arrêtées. Ces arrestations ont été maintenues.
Le rédacteur de la « Freie Zeitungs- et le
conseiller municipal Simond Braunscbweig, de
Soleure, ont pris la fuite.
BALE-VILLE. — Le Grand Conseil a discuté
les interpellations au sujet de la grève. Les
orateurs bourgeois ont attaqué l'attitude conciliante
du gouvernement vis-à-vis des grévistes.
Plusieurs orateurs ont demandé aux membres
bourgeois du Conseil d'Etat de tirer les conséquences
de leur attitude. Les marques d'approbation de
même que les protestations ont été vives dans
la salle et les tribunes.
ARGOVIE. — A Aarau, une réunion d'une
centaine de personnes a décidé do maintenir
l'organisation civique créée dans le but de
défendre la constitution, l'ordre et la liberté
individuelle. Cette organisation sera neutre en
politique, mais désire que toutes mesures soient
prises en vue de relever la situation
économique de toutes les catégories de la population.
La ratification de ces décisions sera demandée
à une assemblée populaire convoquée pour le
24 novembre.
ZURICH. — La motion des grutléens,
adoptée en principe par le Conseil d'Etat et le Grand
Conseil, préconise l'augmeutation du nombre
des membres du Conseil d'Etat à neuf,
l'élection du tribunal suprême et de toutes les
autorités des villes, des districts et des communes
par la proportionnelle, le droit de vote des
femmes, l'introduction de la journée de huit heures
et d'offices de salaires avec force obligatoire, de
l'assurance vieillesse et invalidité, et la
création d'une caisse de retraite du personnel des
services publics et de l'administration judiciaire.
Enfin le postulat insiste sur la réalisation de ces
projets dans le domaine fédéral.
— Le nombre des cas de grippe est
passablement élevé à Zurich. La Tonhalle a été
transformée en hôpital pour les soldats atteints de la
grippe. Environ 300 étudiants en médecine
fonctionnent comme infirmiers volontaires. La
collecte en faveur des soldats malades a déjà
atteint la somme de 200,000 francs.
GENÈVE. — Vendredi, à midi, comme il
descendait du tram au Molard, à Genève, pour se
rendre à son étude, M. Willemin, avocat, maire
de Plainpalais, ex-conseiller national, a été l'
objet d'une violente manifestation de la part de
quelques centaines de citoyens. L'avocat fut
houspillé et évita d'être frappé en courant se
réfugier à son étude, rue Céard, proche du
Molard. La foule s'amassa rapidement dans cette
rue et conspua M. Willemin jusqu'à l'arrivée de
la police qui fut acclamée. Les manifestants se
dispersèrent en criant : < Démission ! A bas
Willemin ! >
Cette manifestation avait été décidée parce
que M. Willemin avait envoyé un télégramme
à Berne demandant la mise en liberté de MM.
Nicolet député socialiste. Hubacher. Hofmanr
et Nicole, arrêtés la veille,. lors des bagarres
de St-Gervais.
— Un violent incendie a détruit, vendredi
matin, un vaste hangar servant d'entrepôt à la
maison Trullas et Cie, primeurs en gros, à
Genève. D'énormes provisions de pommes et
d'oignons ont été détruites. La toiture et toutes les
cuisines d'un immeuble voisin ont
considérablement souffert. Les dégâts dépassent 100,000 fr.
— Le juge d'instruction militaire Rehfous,
après avoir entendu vendredi après midi MM.
Nicolet député socialiste, Hubacher, secrétaire
des métallurgistes, et Hoffmann, président du
parti socialiste genevois, qui avaient été arrêtés
au cours do la bagarre de Coutance, les a remis
en liberté. De son côté, le juge d'instruction
Fulliquet a remis en liberté provisoire plusieurs
manifestants.

SWITZERLAND
A new danger. — The Gazette de Lausanne reports from Bern:

Swiss democracy has emerged with honor from a formidable crisis. Nothing would be more dangerous and deceptive than to imagine that, overnight, we will see our country return to calm and tranquility. We have barely had time to rejoice at the restoration of order when new and more serious dangers threaten us.

According to reliable information that has just reached the Federal Council, the German armies are retreating inland in even greater disorder and anarchy than the Austrian armies after the abrupt cessation of hostilities. These millions of men find their country in complete disintegration: everywhere the regular authorities are being replaced by workers' and soldiers' councils. Officers are completely overwhelmed; all military and civil authority has vanished. The turmoil of minds is terrifying.

These events affect us directly in that masses of soldiers are trying to cross into Switzerland. These are precisely the most dangerous and fanatical elements. In the general confusion, passports are no longer an issue. The men want to cross into Switzerland, willingly or by force, drawn by a very powerful current. The main thing for them is to cross the border by any means, and the workers' and soldiers' councils, far from suppressing this movement, are doing everything in their power to encourage it. These disbanded armies have enthusiastically welcomed the news of the general strike in Switzerland.

The number of those who want to enter our country is estimated at around 80,000.

It goes without saying that we cannot receive them under the conditions in which they present themselves and given the sentiments they express. We have not emerged from the general strike only to fall into even more formidable dangers, if that is possible.

The Federal Council will be obliged to take special measures to protect our country from this invasion, which is anything but peaceful. The events of recent days have shown that our people are firmly resolved to prevent order from being disturbed in our land, in any manner whatsoever. There is no doubt, unfortunately, that the news of this new danger will be welcomed with joy by the organizers of the general strike, who, by all means at their disposal—and they are numerous, varied, and insidious—will seek to exploit this movement to achieve their ends and avenge their failure.

The civic union that instantly formed around the Federal Council and the regular authorities when the hour of danger struck will manifest with the same strength in this new peril. This is all the more indispensable because, in addition to the external front formed by the troops guarding the Rhine border, we will be obliged to establish an internal front against all elements of social disintegration at work within our country.

Diplomatic corps. — Professor Förster has just been appointed, provisionally, as minister of the new Bavarian People's State to the Swiss Confederation.

Having taught for many years at the Federal Polytechnic School and the University of Zurich, Mr. Förster is a faithful friend of our country and knows it well.

Swiss Federal Railways (CFF). — It is learned that the general management of the Swiss Federal Railways has ordered that no storage fees be charged for goods that remained in stations beyond the regulatory deadlines due to the general strike; nor will any delay penalties be charged for wagons that could not be loaded or unloaded in time for the same reason.

Inquiries. — The Federal Council has opened an inquiry into the Bolshevik movement in Switzerland. The Attorney General of the Confederation and the federal examining magistrates are tasked with conducting this inquiry.

The Federal Council has issued special instructions for the judicial inquiry that must identify all those guilty of unlawful acts during the strike.

Grimm and Platten to be prosecuted. — The Federal Council has decided to prosecute Grimm and Platten for organizing a Bolshevik movement in Switzerland.

The cost of the general strike. — The Bund estimates that the losses of all kinds and the expenses due to the three-day general strike amount to between 25 and 30 million francs.

Lausanne Civic Union. — On Saturday evening, at the Montbenon casino, in a very fine and vibrant assembly attended by numerous citizens, the Lausanne Civic Union was established.

Regarding the German consulate in Zurich. — The Gazette de Lausanne learns from Zurich, from a reliable source, that three Germans employed at the German general consulate played an active role in directing the strike.

An irreconcilable. — The Mülhauser Tagblatt reports that Admiral Tirpitz, the promoter of unrestricted submarine warfare, has recently sold his villa in Haslach (Grand Duchy of Baden) and has traveled to Switzerland incognito.

Serious fire. — A fire broke out on Saturday afternoon in the airship hangar at the Bern drill ground. Several captive balloons were seriously damaged.

BERN. — As was the case in Zurich, numerous cases of influenza are reported among the occupation troops mobilized in Bern. A large number of patients are being cared for in the barracks, where volunteer nurses have made themselves available to the military authorities. Among the patients is the commander of the Fribourg regiment, Colonel de Diesbach. The 16th Fribourg battalion left the federal capital on Friday, cheered by the public.

SOLOTHURN. — During the strike incidents in Solothurn and Grenchen, 23 people were arrested. These arrests have been upheld.

The editor of the Freie Zeitung and municipal councilor Simond Braunschweig of Solothurn have fled.

BASEL-CITY. — The Grand Council discussed interpellations regarding the strike. Several speakers demanded that the bourgeois members of the State Council face the consequences of their conciliatory attitude toward the strikers. Both applause and protests were lively in the chamber and the galleries.

LISBON, April 26. — A partial change has just taken place in the cabinet. Mr. d'Oliveira has retired from the finance ministry, accepting the title of Baron of Tojal, and is replaced by Mr. de Carvalho, who had previously been in charge of this department and was president of the chamber of deputies when Don Miguel dissolved it in 1828. The Portuguese cabinet is now, accordingly, composed as follows: da Bandeira, for the navy and foreign affairs; F. Some attempts had been made by Miguelist and Carlist agents in Portugal to incite the people to revolution, but the government's vigilance has thwarted their plans.

Everything is quiet in Lisbon. The marshals and other Chartist officers are expected shortly; their return will be viewed most favorably, especially by the army. It remains to be seen whether the reaction that has begun will stay within constitutional limits.

completion: From ages 9 to 99: the epic theater of science fiction at the Casino de Montbenon. The Théâtre du Levant presents at Montbenon "Head in the Stars," a play conceived and created in 1977 by Maurice Yendt, director of the Théâtre des Jeunes Années in Lyon. Mystery, thrilling adventures, dreams, a touch of poetry, abundant imagination, and a cascade of sensational action—this play brings together all the qualities of epic theater. But this is no longer about musketeers or cowboys; thanks to Mr. Benjamin, we venture onto the cold planet Fulgur. Comic books, television, and cinema have long understood and commercialized young people's enthusiasm for science fiction. War of the planets, Goldorak, robotic friends, fascinating machines capture our children's interest. The genre has its charlatans and geniuses, and it is sometimes difficult to immediately recognize talent amid the sheer volume of productions. Amid this proliferation of adventures, "Head in the Stars" conceals a hint of morality, a pinch of philosophy, a dash of optimism behind the essential sanitized soldiers, conditioned slaves, and all-powerful computer. It is an excellent suspenseful story, a layered adventure where each layer holds a pleasant surprise. And above all, "Head in the Stars" lends itself to the most dynamic staging. Metal bridges, launch platforms, the secret chamber of the Almighty, forbidden underground world, prison, sophisticated Truth-detecting device, alphabetical ray guns XAZE, etc. The Théâtre du Levant, directed by André Fiaux, has created for this futuristic spectacle a mysterious, marvelous set, as fascinating and intricate as an alchemist's alembic. The costumes, designed by Mouky, admirably respect space-age fashion, and the accessories by Henri Barbier and Maria Estève are intriguing enough that, by the end of the show, young and older alike rush onto the stage to understand, touch, and explore these new gadgets. This dynamic spectacle is well supported by a team of experienced actors: versatile performers, each plays multiple characters and contributed to the set design. With Gisèle Ratzé, Pascal Dayer, Alain Nitchacff, Eric Mathyer, André Fiaux, and the very endearing Rodolphe Ittig in the role of Mr. Benjamin. P. Ruffieux Casino de Montbenon, Paderewsky Hall, Saturday, December 12 at 2 p.m.

This dynamic spectacle is well supported by a team of experienced actors: versatile performers, each plays multiple characters and contributed to the set design. With Gisèle Ratzé, Pascal Dayer, Alain Nitchacff, Eric Mathyer, André Fiaux, and the very endearing Rodolphe Ittig in the role of Mr. Benjamin. P. Ruffieux Casino de Montbenon, Paderewsky Hall, Saturday, December 12 at 2 p.m.

The Divide

This concerns the divide that, alas! is widening between German-speaking Swiss and French-speaking Swiss. It prompts Mr. E. Juillerat, in the "Jura" of Porrentruy, to offer these useful reflections aimed at proposing a remedy:

We believe that a favorable reaction would be the development of a very precise and especially very clear federalist program, a program that would not be merely verbal. Words, in fact, no longer carry weight... given the contempt observed when, in parliamentary assemblies, French-speaking voices simply demand the safeguarding of legitimate cantonal freedoms.

If one wishes to avoid worsening the unease, the widening of a divide likely to harm the good spirit of concord at a time when it proves so necessary, action must be taken.

Concord? It will not be established through bullying. It cannot be obtained by means of capitulation, because everything in French-speaking Switzerland that has a sense of patriotic dignity and rightful pride will never subscribe to it.

Unfortunately, there will be eager courtiers willing to sell not only their rights but those of their fellow citizens for a mess of pottage of substantial advantages. There will also be doctrinaires followed by faithful followers who will cheaply trade traditions, the true principles of law, to applaud anything favoring a unification constituting a peril for Switzerland.

But the mass of French-speaking Swiss, if well guided, if clearly shown the positions to defend, the heritage to preserve, will not hesitate to say once and for all: stop! to a majority, to a Federal Council lacking the proper notion of the respect it deserves and the rights conferred upon it by the charter of the country itself.

Therefore, it is now important to ensure cohesion, to set, to establish a plan of action absolutely free from foolish attacks, leaving bridges intact, but inspired by a firmly resolved will against a unification that would lead to tyranny. Already now, while the majority feels the country threatened by foreign mystiques, it only knows how to display an intransigence provoking the most painful friction.

What would it be from the moment when all the dams still maintained by federalism had been undermined?

Let the French-speaking minority therefore act energetically to save not only its rights but the country itself. It is time.

A Singular Representative of the People

In a press release, the Swiss National Action recalls the singular past of Humbert-Droz, who has just acceded to the National Council.

This man, judged worthy of sitting in the Swiss Parliament, played a leading role at the sixth congress of the Communist International in 1928. He was, with the sinister Bukharin, the reporter of the session where the "Presidium" of the Comintern was elected. There he presented the candidates on behalf of the Comintern leadership and was himself designated to be part of it. He displayed great activity until the end of 1928. At the ninth session of the executive committee of the Communist International, he was entrusted with the report, of particular importance, on the trade union question.

Until the end of 1928, Humbert-Droz was thus one of the prominent men in the leadership of the Comintern. He subsequently fell into disgrace, along with Bukharin, Rykov, and Tomsky, under the pretext of having "deviated to the right." The first two were executed in 1938; Tomsky had committed suicide.

In a subsequent letter addressed to the Comintern, Humbert-Droz humbly acknowledged that the Presidium had been "right to condemn his declaration of December 1928 as hypocritically opportunistic and as an unworthy attack against the Communist International." Even better: on October 19, 1930, Humbert-Droz made an act of complete submission to the Comintern leadership. The conclusion of his apology—if one can call it that—is formulated as follows: "I declare to the Presidium that I cease all ideological opposition and that, henceforth, I will apply its policy not only out of discipline, but fundamentally convinced that it is the only possible, the only revolutionary, and consequently the only right one in the present situation."

This declaration provides irrefutable proof of the servility of Humbert-Droz towards Stalin, whose orders he will henceforth execute. The leaders of the Comintern, sure of his fidelity, sent him back to Switzerland to discipline the communist party and perfect its revolutionary action. Invested with this mission of trust, Humbert-Droz demonstrated the same submission to Moscow. He humbly accepts the admonitions of his foreign masters and executes all their orders. Appointed secretary of the party, he applies himself to implementing the decisions of the Communist International congress, organizes courses for the training of propaganda agents, and works with all his strength to reestablish a Swiss Popular Front. When his former friends and chiefs of the Russian communist party are savagely tortured and executed by Stalin, Humbert-Droz approves the tyrant and has articles glorifying the Moscow massacres published in the party press.

These revelations, which every Swiss ought to ponder, are taken from the "International Correspondence" of May 15, 1928 and December 8, 1930.

Romania and the Germans of the Sudetenland

It is interesting to see how Romania, one of the countries of the Little Entente, reacts to German agitation in Czechoslovakia. "The Romanian Independence" comments on Mr. Henlein's speech at the congress of the Sudeten German Party in Karlsbad and writes the following:

The intentions of Mr. Henlein, as they appear in his Karlsbad speech, aim to put Nietzsche's teaching on the revaluation of all values into practice, and this with the help of the Prague government. First, through internal decomposition, he wishes to make Czechoslovakia renounce its own foreign policy. His comparison with Switzerland cannot be made. On one hand, there are no internal conflicts in that country, and on the other, that country's policy of neutrality cannot oblige it to renounce anything regarding a neighboring state. Everything suggests that Mr. Henlein is an unwilling idealist who wants to make his homeland a paradise. But if he believes in poets and philosophers, he is merely an executor of others' ideas.

On the other hand, in the organ of the former Undersecretary of State Gafenco, "Timpul," we read, under the title "From William Tell to Henlein," the following article:

Mr. Henlein demands more than a unified legal statute, which, moreover, the Czechoslovak government in all loyalty, but naturally within the framework of the legal organization of the centralized state, is already preparing. Mr. Henlein demands a federative state, following the example of Switzerland, thus a new political and not legal order. But, a German-speaking Swiss is first and foremost a citizen of Switzerland. His national ideal is the freedom and independence of Switzerland. This heritage from his ancestors, he is determined to defend against all. There is no idea more foreign to a Swiss, citizen of a federative state with four languages, than the idea of race. This idea would be the death of a federative state. But, Mr. Henlein wants a state that would be federative like Switzerland and racist like Germany. He demands that the new state pursue a policy favorable to the Reich's "Drang nach Osten." The minority would be autonomous, while the majority would be obliged to follow the totalitarian policy of the minority.

In Henlein's "Switzerland," Gessler's hat still exists and William Tell has not yet made his appearance... Le fossé
Il s'agit du fossé qui, hélas ! se

Nous croyons qu'une heureuse
réaction serait la mise au point d'un
programme fédéraliste très précis et surtout
très clair, programme qui ne serait pas
seulement verbal. Les mots, en effet,

mépris que l'on constate lorsque s'élèvent,
dans les assemblées parlementaires, des
voix romandes revendiquant simplement
la sauvegarde des légitimes libertés
cantonales.
Si l'on veut éviter l'aggravation du
malaise, l'élargissement d'un fossé de
nature à nuire au bon esprit de
concorde au moment où 11 s'avère si
nécessaire, il faut agir.
La concorde ? Elle ne s'établira pas
sur des brimades. On ne pourra
l'obtenir au moyen d'une capitulation, car
tout ce qui a, en Suisse romande, le sens

fierté, n'y souscrira Jamais.
Malheureusement il y aura des

contre le plat de lentilles d'avantages
substantiels non seulement leurs droits, mais

qui feront bon marché des traditions,

Mais la masse des Romands, si elle est

Inspiré d'une volonté fermement résolue

la majorité sent le pays menacé par les
mystiques étrangères, elle ne sait faire

provoquant les plus douloureux froissements.
Qu'en serait-il dès le moment où toutes
les digues que maintient encore le

Que la minorité romande agisse donc
énergiquement pour sauver non

est temps.
Un singulier représentant
du peuple

communiste, en 1928. Il fut, avec le sinistre
Boukharine, rapporteur de la séance où
fut élu le « Présldium » du Komintern.
Il y a présenté les candidats au nom de
la direction du Komintern et a été
luimême désigné pour en faire partie. H y

fin de l'année 1928. A la neuvième

Jusqu'à la fin de 1928, Humbert-Droz
fut donc l'un des hommes en vue de
la direction du Komintern. H tomba

Rykoff et Tomsky, sous prétexte d'avoir

Dans une lettre ultérieure, adressée au

opportuniste et comme étant une
attaque indigne contre l'Internationale
communiste ». Bien mieux : le 19
octobre 1930, Humbert-Droz fit acte de
soumlslon complète envers la direction du
Komintern. La conclusion de son
amende honorable — si l'on peut dire —
est formulée comme suit : « Je déclare
au Présldium que Je cesse toute
opposition Idéologique et que, dorénavant,
J'appliquerai sa politique non seulement
par discipline, mais foncièrement
convaincu qu'elle est la seule possible, la

Il accepte humblement les admonesta »
tlons de ses maîtres étrangers et en

taire du parti, 11 s'applique à mettre en

pagande et travaille de toutes ses forces
à rétablissement d'un Front populaire
suisse. Lorsque ses anciens amis et oheft

Humbert-Droz approuve le tyran et fait
publier dans la presse du parti des
articles à la gloire des massacreurs de

Ces révélations, que tout Suisse se doit
de méditer, sont empruntées à la « Cor »
respondance Internationale » des 15 ma ™
1928 et 8 décembre 1930.
La Roumanie
et les Allemands des _Sudèted
77 est intéressant de voir comment
la Roumanie, un des pays de la
tite-Entente, réagit en face de l'agi _,
tation allemande en
Tchécoslovaquie. « L'Indépendance roumaine *
commente le discours de M. Henlein.
au congrès du parti des Allemands
des Sudètes à Karlsbad et écrit ce
qui suit :
Les intentions de M. Henlein, telles
qu'elles apparaissent dans son discours
de Karlsbad, ont pour but de mettre en
pratique l'enseignement de Nietzsche sm
la revalorisation de toutes les valeurs et
cela avec l'aide du gouvernement de
Prague. Tout d'abord, par une
décomposition intérieure, 11 désire faire renoncer
la Tchécoslovaquie à sa politique
extérieure propre. Sa comparaison avec la
Suisse ne peut se faire. D'une part, 11
n'y a pas de conflits Intérieurs dans ce
pays et, d'autre part, la politique de
neutralité de ce pays ne peut l'obliger
de renoncer à quoi que ce soit à l'égard
d'un Etat voisin. Tout fait croire que
M. Henlein est un idéaliste malgré lui
qui veut faire de sa patrie un paradis.
Mais s'il croit aux poètes et aux
philosophes, il n'est qu'un exécuteur des
Idées des autres.
D'autre part, dans l'organe de
l'ancien sous-secrétaire d'Etat
_Gafenco, « Timpul », nous lisons, sous
le titre : « De Guillaume Tell à
Henlein », l'article suivant :
M. Henlein demande plus qu'un statut
juridique unifié, ce que d'ailleurs le
gouvernement tchécoslovaque en toute
loyauté, mais naturellement dans H
cadre de l'organisation Juridique de
l'Etat centralisé, prépare déjà. M.
Henlein demande un Etat fédératif, selon
l'exemple de la Suisse, donc un nouvel
ordre politique et non juridique. Mais,
un Suisse alémanique est avant tout un
citoyen de la Suisse. Son idéal national
est la liberté et l'indépendance de la
Suisse. Ce bien, hérité de ses ancêtres,
U est décidé de le défendre contre tous.
H n'y a pas d'idée qui serait plus
étrangère à un Suisse, citoyen d'un Etat
fédératif à quatre langues que l'idée de
race. Cette Idée serait la mort d'un Etat
fédératif. Mais, M. Henlein veut un Etat
qui serait fédératif comme la Suisse et
raciste comme l'Allemagne. H demande
que le nouvel Etat fasse une politique
qui soit favorable au « Drang nach Osten »
du Reich. La minorité serait autonome,
tandis que la majorité serait obligée de
faire la politique totalitaire de la
minorité.
Dans « la Suisse » de Henlein, _Ij
chapeau de Gessler existe encore et
Guillaume Tell n'a pas encore fait son
apparition... Pour nous, qui suivons aveo
toute l'attention nécessaire l'expansion
allemande vers l'est, le discours de M.
Henlein est spécialement significatif.
Notre pensée amicale est maintenant
pour ce pays qui ne provoque personne,
qui désire la paix et qui, malgré tout,
est forcé de défendre avec toute la
volonté l'idée de son Indépendance
politique et économique : la Tchécoslovaquie.

The Divide

This concerns the divide that, alas! is widening between German-speaking Swiss and French-speaking Swiss. It prompts Mr. E. Juillerat, in the "Jura" of Porrentruy, to offer these useful reflections aimed at proposing a remedy:

We believe that a favorable reaction would be the development of a very precise and especially very clear federalist program, a program that would not be merely verbal. Words, in fact, no longer carry weight... given the contempt observed when, in parliamentary assemblies, French-speaking voices simply demand the safeguarding of legitimate cantonal freedoms.

If one wishes to avoid worsening the unease, the widening of a divide likely to harm the good spirit of concord at a time when it proves so necessary, action must be taken.

Concord? It will not be established through bullying. It cannot be obtained by means of capitulation, because everything in French-speaking Switzerland that has a sense of patriotic dignity and rightful pride will never subscribe to it.

Unfortunately, there will be eager courtiers willing to sell not only their rights but those of their fellow citizens for a mess of pottage of substantial advantages. There will also be doctrinaires followed by faithful followers who will cheaply trade traditions, the true principles of law, to applaud anything favoring a unification constituting a peril for Switzerland.

But the mass of French-speaking Swiss, if well guided, if clearly shown the positions to defend, the heritage to preserve, will not hesitate to say once and for all: stop! to a majority, to a Federal Council lacking the proper notion of the respect it deserves and the rights conferred upon it by the charter of the country itself.

Therefore, it is now important to ensure cohesion, to set, to establish a plan of action absolutely free from foolish attacks, leaving bridges intact, but inspired by a firmly resolved will against a unification that would lead to tyranny. Already now, while the majority feels the country threatened by foreign mystiques, it only knows how to display an intransigence provoking the most painful friction.

What would it be from the moment when all the dams still maintained by federalism had been undermined?

Let the French-speaking minority therefore act energetically to save not only its rights but the country itself. It is time.

A Singular Representative of the People

In a press release, the Swiss National Action recalls the singular past of Humbert-Droz, who has just acceded to the National Council.

This man, judged worthy of sitting in the Swiss Parliament, played a leading role at the sixth congress of the Communist International in 1928. He was, with the sinister Bukharin, the reporter of the session where the "Presidium" of the Comintern was elected. There he presented the candidates on behalf of the Comintern leadership and was himself designated to be part of it. He displayed great activity until the end of 1928. At the ninth session of the executive committee of the Communist International, he was entrusted with the report, of particular importance, on the trade union question.

Until the end of 1928, Humbert-Droz was thus one of the prominent men in the leadership of the Comintern. He subsequently fell into disgrace, along with Bukharin, Rykov, and Tomsky, under the pretext of having "deviated to the right." The first two were executed in 1938; Tomsky had committed suicide.

In a subsequent letter addressed to the Comintern, Humbert-Droz humbly acknowledged that the Presidium had been "right to condemn his declaration of December 1928 as hypocritically opportunistic and as an unworthy attack against the Communist International." Even better: on October 19, 1930, Humbert-Droz made an act of complete submission to the Comintern leadership. The conclusion of his apology—if one can call it that—is formulated as follows: "I declare to the Presidium that I cease all ideological opposition and that, henceforth, I will apply its policy not only out of discipline, but fundamentally convinced that it is the only possible, the only revolutionary, and consequently the only right one in the present situation."

This declaration provides irrefutable proof of the servility of Humbert-Droz towards Stalin, whose orders he will henceforth execute. The leaders of the Comintern, sure of his fidelity, sent him back to Switzerland to discipline the communist party and perfect its revolutionary action. Invested with this mission of trust, Humbert-Droz demonstrated the same submission to Moscow. He humbly accepts the admonitions of his foreign masters and executes all their orders. Appointed secretary of the party, he applies himself to implementing the decisions of the Communist International congress, organizes courses for the training of propaganda agents, and works with all his strength to reestablish a Swiss Popular Front. When his former friends and chiefs of the Russian communist party are savagely tortured and executed by Stalin, Humbert-Droz approves the tyrant and has articles glorifying the Moscow massacres published in the party press.

These revelations, which every Swiss ought to ponder, are taken from the "International Correspondence" of May 15, 1928 and December 8, 1930.

Romania and the Germans of the Sudetenland

It is interesting to see how Romania, one of the countries of the Little Entente, reacts to German agitation in Czechoslovakia. "The Romanian Independence" comments on Mr. Henlein's speech at the congress of the Sudeten German Party in Karlsbad and writes the following:

The intentions of Mr. Henlein, as they appear in his Karlsbad speech, aim to put Nietzsche's teaching on the revaluation of all values into practice, and this with the help of the Prague government. First, through internal decomposition, he wishes to make Czechoslovakia renounce its own foreign policy. His comparison with Switzerland cannot be made. On one hand, there are no internal conflicts in that country, and on the other, that country's policy of neutrality cannot oblige it to renounce anything regarding a neighboring state. Everything suggests that Mr. Henlein is an unwilling idealist who wants to make his homeland a paradise. But if he believes in poets and philosophers, he is merely an executor of others' ideas.

On the other hand, in the organ of the former Undersecretary of State Gafenco, "Timpul," we read, under the title "From William Tell to Henlein," the following article:

Mr. Henlein demands more than a unified legal statute, which, moreover, the Czechoslovak government in all loyalty, but naturally within the framework of the legal organization of the centralized state, is already preparing. Mr. Henlein demands a federative state, following the example of Switzerland, thus a new political and not legal order. But, a German-speaking Swiss is first and foremost a citizen of Switzerland. His national ideal is the freedom and independence of Switzerland. This heritage from his ancestors, he is determined to defend against all. There is no idea more foreign to a Swiss, citizen of a federative state with four languages, than the idea of race. This idea would be the death of a federative state. But, Mr. Henlein wants a state that would be federative like Switzerland and racist like Germany. He demands that the new state pursue a policy favorable to the Reich's "Drang nach Osten." The minority would be autonomous, while the majority would be obliged to follow the totalitarian policy of the minority.

In Henlein's "Switzerland," Gessler's hat still exists and William Tell has not yet made his appearance... For us, who follow with all necessary attention German expansion towards the east, Mr. Henlein's speech is especially significant. Our friendly thought is now for this country that provokes no one, desires peace, and yet, despite everything, is forced to defend with all its will the idea of its political and economic independence: Czechoslovakia.

THE WAR
The French Front
PARIS, 9:15 AM. — Between Montdidier and the Oise, the French conducted a local operation west of Anteuil on a front of nearly 4 kilometers.
The French troops, supported by assault tanks, penetrated the German lines, captured Porte Farm and Les Loges Farm; they achieved an advance of 1,800 meters at certain points. A German counterattack at Les Loges Farm was repelled; the French maintained all their gains.
The number of prisoners currently counted reaches 450, including 14 officers.
South of the Aisne, artillery continued to be active during the night in the region of Chavigny Farm; the French intensified their progress at this point, and they took about twenty prisoners, including one officer.
Activity from both artilleries west and north of Château-Thierry, notably at Hill 204.
Patrols brought back prisoners in Champagne, in the Marquise sector and towards Souain Hill.
Nothing to report on the rest of the front.

LONDON, 9:00 PM. — During the night, London's troops executed a successful raid east of Arras and captured some prisoners and a machine gun. Enemy artillery was active against the positions we recently captured south of the Somme.

BERLIN, 9:00 AM. — Army Group of Crown Prince Rupprecht. — South of the La Bassée Canal, partial attacks, repeated several times, as well as on the north bank of the Somme, strong enemy pushes were repelled. Artillery combat remained lively in these sectors and became violent at times towards evening on both sides of the Somme.
Army Group of the German Crown Prince. — West of Autheuil (southwest of Noyon) local enemy attacks developed this morning after heavy shelling. Near the forest of Villers-Cotterêts, partial French enterprises in our combat zone failed.

BERLIN, 9:00 PM. — Near Noyon, partial French attacks were repelled. Local combat crowned with success west of Château-Thierry.

While operations have become almost negligible on the Italian front, it seems that the Balkan front is regaining interest, at least in Albania, where the Italians, aided by the French and English monitors, are achieving successes on the banks of the Vjosë.

VIENNA, 9:00 AM. — In Albania, the energetic pressure of enemy forces, advancing beyond the Vjosë, continues. Southwest of Berat, some engagements. In connection with these combat actions, the French have gained ground on the upper Devoll.

ROME, 9:00 AM. — Our action, begun on the left wing after a fire preparation in which the monitors of the British navy effectively participated, continues.
The infantry, starting from the lower Vjosë, cleared the heights between Levani and Posani Monastery of enemies after a fierce struggle, while the cavalry, passing between the western slopes of Malakastra and the sea, boldly advanced on the enemy's rear and cut the bridges over the Seman at Metan. The locality of Bier has fallen into our hands.
In the center, the very strong positions of Çafa e Glavës and Korçof, fiercely defended by the enemy, are in our possession.
At the head of the Tomorrica, we have seized the contested height of Çafa e Devris.
Our airplanes and the British provided valuable assistance to the struggle! The number of prisoners rose to more than 1,300. The capture of an undetermined number of cannons and machine guns and significant booty is reported.

FRANKFURT, 9:00 AM. — According to the Berlin correspondent of the "Frankfurter Zeitung," it was announced on Tuesday in the Reichstag that Mr. von Kühlmann, State Minister, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, has been placed on leave. Mr. Hintze, who for a year has been Germany's minister plenipotentiary in Christiania, is mentioned as his successor.
The Reichstag immediately sent the credit bill to the central committee to deliberate on the political consequences of Mr. von Kühlmann's retirement. Under the present circumstances, it is declared that an adjournment of the Reichstag cannot be considered.
This resignation is officially explained by Mr. von Kühlmann's attitude during the discussion on the credits. But his position had been singularly compromised since his speech of June 25. He had declared, in fact, as one recalls, "that there was no reason to expect an absolute end to the war by purely military decisions outside of all diplomatic negotiations."

BERLIN, 9:00 AM (Wolff). — It is announced from an authoritative source that the Emperor has accepted the resignation presented by Secretary of State von Kühlmann. His successor has been designated in the person of the current ambassador to Christiania, Hintze. The definitive decision has nevertheless not yet been taken.

HELSINKI, 8:00 AM. — The Diet adopted in second reading the law for punishing insurgents and voted by 65 votes against 36 to send the insurgents to forced labor abroad. (In Germany, of course.) The government declared that maintaining 40,000 prisoners would cost over 100 million and require 4,000 guards, equivalent to a class of recruits.

STOCKHOLM, 8:00 AM. — The Finnish chargé d'affaires in Berlin is en route to Helsinki. He will probably propose to the Senate to choose Prince Oscar of Prussia as King of Finland. Faced with republican opposition, the Germanophiles are still considering imposing a monarchical regime by a coup d'état.

completion:
ATHLETICS: Bikila returns to Rome, but not barefoot!  
Olympic marathon champion Abebe Bikila arrived in Rome late Thursday morning from Addis Ababa to attend the world premiere of the film "The Great Olympics" at the Opera Theatre, featuring footage shot during the Rome Games.  
The Olympic champion is a guest of Mr. Romolo Marcellini, the film's director, who invited him on the very day of his marathon victory.

FOOTBALL: English strike averted  
An agreement was reached on Wednesday evening at the British Ministry of Labour in London between the Football League and English professional players: the footballers' strike, scheduled for next Saturday, will therefore not take place.  
This decision was made after an hour and a half of discussions between Mr. John Hare, the Minister of Labour, and representatives of the League and the professional players.  
The Swiss Sport-Toto competition on January 21 will proceed as normal.

SHOOTING: Death of Mr. F. Stirnimann  
Mr. Franz Stirnimann, founder of a major construction machinery factory that bears his name, passed away in Olten at the age of 76, after several years of declining health.  
The deceased played a leading role in the development of small-bore shooting, of which he was one of the most ardent advocates, and he still chaired the press commission of the Swiss Small-Bore Shooting Association.  
Mr. Franz Stirnimann recently demonstrated his commitment to our national sport par excellence by donating his magnificent property on the Lucerne Lido to the Swiss Rifle Society, which was transformed a few months ago into the "Shooters' House."  
It will likely soon become the headquarters of the Swiss Shooting Federation.  
Former world champion W. Lienhard currently resides there as curator.  
Mr. Stirnimann, a loyal and tirelessly dedicated man, richly deserved the honors bestowed upon him by Swiss shooters.

CYCLING: Dr. Stern, director of the rehabilitation clinic in Lamalou-les-Bains, visited Roger Rivière, whom he had treated first after his fall in the Tour de France.  
"You still need six months of careful treatment," he told the hour record holder.

Watchmaking: cautious optimism  
GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF "SWISS WATCHMAKING INFORMATION"  
Chaux-de-Fonds, August (ATS). – Prospects for the watchmaking industry must be viewed with cautious and measured optimism. This was stated by President Charles-Maurice Wittwer in his presidential address on Wednesday during the general assembly of "Swiss Watchmaking Information," held in Chaux-de-Fonds. At first glance, he said, the current year should allow the watchmaking industry to consolidate its positions and achieve results comparable to those of 1980. However, any forecast is difficult, given the uncertainties that remain regarding monetary developments and the direction of the global economic situation. Finally, the resurgence of protectionist tendencies imposes an additional burden on the development of global trade.  

In his economic overview, Mr. Wittwer emphasized that the situation of the watchmaking industry, considered overall, improved in 1980. The clearly rising curve of exports of electronic products is particularly encouraging. However, standard and low-end items, which represent a large part of production, still face difficulties, notably due to strong competition from cheap products, which Southeast Asia floods certain markets. The speaker regretted that certain "instruments" made available to exporters to help them remain competitive have been demobilized, or their use made more costly, precisely when a new increase in costs, particularly wages, occurred. On the other hand, he welcomed the decision by which the Federal Council has just extended, in a spirit of continuity, the coverage of short-term exchange risk by the export risk guarantee.  

Mr. Wittwer also recalled that the extension of official quality control is on a good path, while noting the necessity that it goes hand in hand with the revision of the ordinance governing the use of the designation "Swiss made," whose value should be strengthened.  

Regarding statutory decisions, the general assembly of Swiss Watchmaking Information re-elected Mr. Charles-Maurice Wittwer as president for a period of three years.

Le règne de Liverpool se terminern-t-il ce soir ?
La période de domination de Liverpool en coupe d'Europe des clubs champions
pourrait se terminer ce soir, à I'Anfield Road, quand les champions de 1977 et 1978,
recevront Nottingham Forest, champion d'Angleterre, en match retour du premier tour
de cette compétition.
Liverpool a été battu par 2-0 lors du
match aller, il y a deux semaines, à
tingham, et les chances de l'équipe de Bob
Paisley de remonter un tel handicap,
contre un club qui n'a encaissé que cinq
buts dans ses sept premiers matches cette
saison, semblent plutôt minces, d'autant
plus que la victoire de l'équipe de Brian
Clough à Nottinhgam semble avoir porté
un coup au moral de Liverpool.
MILIEU DE TERRAIN NEUTRALISÉ
C'est ainsi, par exemple, que samedi
dernier, Liverpool a concédé son premier
point en championnat (face à West
Bromwich Albion) et qu'il peut même
s'estimer heureux d'avoir arraché le
match nul grâce à un but de 1 opportuniste
écossais Kenny Dalglish.
Comme Nottingham Forest, l '«
Albion » a maîtrisé Liverpool en
neutralisant le jeu de son milieu de terrain.
C'est ainsi que Souness, Kennedy et
McDermott, n'ont pu se « promener »
comme ils l'avaient fait contre le FC
Bruges, en finale de la Coupe des clubs
champions, à Wembley, en mai dernier, et
bien d'autres fois...
DES PROBLÈMES
De plus, Liverpool a d'autres
problèmes. Les défenseurs de l'équipe
d'Angleterre, Phil Neal et Emlyn Hughes, et
l'ailier Steve Heigh way (Eire) ont perdS la
forme. Les deux premiers ont été
décevants contre le Danemark, la semaine
dernière, à Copenhague, et Heighway a
été remplacé aussi bien contre l'Irlande, à
Dublin, que contre West Bromwich
Albion, samedi dernier. Il est possible que
Paisley retienne David Johnson ou le
« super-remplaçant » David Fairclough
pour remplacer l'international irlandais.
De son côté, le « Forest » devra jouer
sans son arrière gauche, Colin Barrett,
blessé samedi dernier. Son remplaçant
sera probablement Frank Clark, un
« vétéran » de trente-trois ans, mais
McLough pourrait créer une nouvelle
surprise, comme par exemple l'éviction
de son « stratège » Archie Gemmill, la
semaine dernière.
NOUVELLE VEDETTE
McLough pourra, par contre, aligner sa
nouvelle « vedette », l'avant-centre Gary
Birtles, un débutant qui a remplacé Peter
White (le « buteur » de l'équipe de l'an
dernier) avec tant de succès. Birtles
marqua le premier but du « Forest » face à
Liverpool il y a quinze jours et fut à
l'origine du second.
L'équipe de Liverpool aura donc une
tâche très difficile à remplir si elle veut
poursuivre sa carrière en coupe d'Europe.
Elle compte également, pour réussir, sur
l'appui que ne manqueront pas de lui
apporter ses fanatiques « supporters ».
La composition probable des équipes :
Liverpool (4-4-2) : Clémence —
Neal, Thompson, Hugues (Cap), Alan
Kennedy.-Cas, McDermott, Souness,
Ray Kennedy.-Dalglish, Johnson (
Fairclough).
Nottingham Forest (4-3-3) : Shilton.
Anderson, Burns, Lloyd, Clark (O'Hare).
-O'Neill, McGovern, Bowyer (Gemmill)
— Woodcock, Birtles, Robertson.

The European Cup holder struggling against Nottingham Forest  
Will Liverpool's reign end tonight?  
Liverpool's period of dominance in the European Cup for champions could come to an end tonight at Anfield Road, when the 1977 and 1978 champions host Nottingham Forest, the English champions, in the return match of the first round of this competition.

Liverpool was beaten 2-0 in the first match two weeks ago in Nottingham, and the chances of Bob Paisley's team overcoming such a deficit against a club that has conceded only five goals in its first seven matches this season seem rather slim, especially since Brian Clough's team's victory in Nottingham appears to have dealt a blow to Liverpool's morale.

MIDFIELD NEUTRALIZED  
This is how, for example, last Saturday Liverpool conceded its first point in the league (against West Bromwich Albion) and can even consider itself lucky to have snatched a draw thanks to a goal from the opportunistic Scottish player Kenny Dalglish.

Like Nottingham Forest, "Albion" controlled Liverpool by neutralizing its midfield play. This is how Souness, Kennedy, and McDermott could not "roam" as they had done against FC Bruges in the final of the European Cup for champions at Wembley last May, and many other times...

PROBLEMS  
Moreover, Liverpool has other problems. The defenders of the England team, Phil Neal and Emlyn Hughes, and the winger Steve Heighway (Ireland) have lost their form. The first two were disappointing against Denmark last week in Copenhagen, and Heighway was replaced both against Ireland in Dublin and against West Bromwich Albion last Saturday. It is possible that Paisley will select David Johnson or the "super-substitute" David Fairclough to replace the Irish international.

On its side, "Forest" will have to play without its left back, Colin Barrett, injured last Saturday. His replacement will likely be Frank Clark, a "veteran" of thirty-three years, but McLough could create a new surprise, such as the exclusion of his "strategist" Archie Gemmill last week.

NEW STAR  
McLough, however, can field his new "star," the center forward Gary Birtles, a newcomer who replaced Peter White (the "scorer" of last year's team) with such success. Birtles scored the first goal for "Forest" against Liverpool two weeks ago and was responsible for the second.

Liverpool's team therefore faces a very difficult task if it wants to continue its career in the European Cup. It also relies, for success, on the support that its fanatical "supporters" will undoubtedly provide.

The probable team compositions:  
Liverpool (4-4-2): Clemence — Neal, Thompson, Hughes (Capt.), Alan Kennedy — Case, McDermott, Souness, Ray Kennedy — Dalglish, Johnson (or Fairclough).  
Nottingham Forest (4-3-3): Shilton — Anderson, Burns, Lloyd, Clark (or O'Hare) — O'Neill, McGovern, Bowyer (or Gemmill) — Woodcock, Birtles, Robertson.

Images troubles
La Suisse au regard du monde : entre réalité et fiction
Dans son Essai sur les Révolutions, Chateaubriand écrit en
1797 que « les Scythes, dans le monde ancien, les Suisses,
dans le monde moderne, attirèrent les yeux de leurs
contemporains par la célébrité de leur innocence. »
Manfred Gsteiger
Une telle remarque est pour ainsi dire
le résumé d'innombrables discours,
littéraires et autres, de l'Europe des
Lumières et de la sensibilité préromantique où
la Suisse apparaît comme le lieu
idyllique d'une nature et d'une humanité
non conompues et la patrie de toutes
les vertus républicaines. Et pourtant, à
la même époque, Goethe note dans ses
Lettres écrites de la Suisse que le mythe
de la liberté helvétique n'est qu'un
« vieux conte pour enfants conservé
dans de l'esprit de vin », et un autre
voyageur allemand, Christian
Hirschfeld, se plaint en 1776 de l'immoralité
et de l'ivrognerie des Suisses.
Caricatures
Sans doute n'avons-nous pas fini de
vivre avec ce genre d'images
contradictoires où la vérité et la fiction, les clichés
idéalisants et les caricatures grotesques
se mélangent et s'entrecroisent de
façon déconcertante, qu'il s'agisse d'
autostéréotypes ou d'hétérostéréotypes,
c'est-à-dire de portraits- " types » peints
par les Suisses eux-mêmes ou vus de
l'extérieur. Cela va, comme le dit
ges-André Chevallaz, « de la marche
triomphale à la dodécaphonie ». Et si la
plupart de nos politiciens et nos
rhé-SUISSE ROMANTIQUE-Le mythe de la pureté et de l'innocence.
a-far
teurs officiels ont toujours et encore la
fâcheuse tendance de souligner qu'il
n'y en a point comme nous, la majorité
des écrivains, véritable « opposition
tra-parlementaire », tient à nous
rappeler sans cesse que nous vivons dans
une société égoïste, dans le paradis du
matérialisme et du conformisme stérile.
Quant aux observateurs étrangers,
force nous est d'admettre qu'ils sont de
moins en moins enclins, et pour cause,
à nous identifier avec le pays ouvert,
hospitalier et courageux dont nous
voudrions perpétuer le souvenir...
A cet égard, une publication récente
de la Nouvelle Société Helvétique
intitulée La Suisse et le monde est pleine
d'intérêt. Non seulement parce qu'elle
pose le problème de notre intégration
dans une Europe qui est malgré tout en
train de se faire, sans nous et presque
contre nous (on n'oubliera pas qu'en
1992 les barrières douanières doivent
tomber), mais parce qu'elle nous
propose une série d'images de la Suisse
qui ont de quoi nous faire réfléchir.
Ainsi le Français Lionel Richard, qui
constate que « les quelques aspects
positifs que pouvait présenter l'image de la
Suisse en France se sont dégradés » et
qui s'interroge sur « cet étonnant
cloisonnement » de la Suisse romande.
Ou Helmut-Maria Glogger, journaliste
allemand vivant à Zurich, qui, tout en
déclarant « J'aime la Suisse », stigmatise
notre autosatisfaction. Contre cette
autosatisfaction, 1 écrivain bâlois Urs
Widmer préconise le séjour prolongé à
l'étranger, lui-même Suisse de l'étranger
rentré au pays où il retrouve notre
symbole national, la vache.
D'autres écrivains suisses sont plus
agressifs ; Claude Jaquillard déclare
« Mieux vaut être Européen, vivant,
révolutionnaire et conquérant que Suisse _,
neutre, protégé, prévoyant et mort » _,
tandis que le Tessinois Dante Andréa
Franzetti, détenteur de deux passeports _,
se réclame de son héritage italien
contre un « suissisme » étroit.
Tare du système
Il y a, bien sûr, des avis plus
pondérés, et l'ancien conseiller fédéral ne
manque pas de prôner l '« osmose rai
sonnable et constante entre économie
et politique » que d'autres considèrent
comme la tare de notre système. Mais i
n'est pas sûr que la bonne conscience
même de M. Chevallaz soit _, sans faille
Pourquoi parlerait-il du « poids d'un
conformisme social parfois plus lourd
que celui des lois »?
Les avis exprimés dans ces témoigna
ges sont loin d'être unanimes. Il s'er
dégage tout de même l'image d'un pays
en crise d'identité. Est-ce-là une fiction
de gens de lettres (encore une) ou la
réalité ? La question est posée, il n'y e
pas moyen de l'éviter.
M. G

Images Troubles
Switzerland in the Eyes of the World: Between Reality and Fiction

In his Essay on Revolutions, Chateaubriand wrote in 1797 that "the Scythians, in the ancient world, and the Swiss, in the modern world, attracted the eyes of their contemporaries by the fame of their innocence."

Manfred Gsteiger

Such a remark is, so to speak, the summary of countless literary and other discourses from the Europe of the Enlightenment and pre-Romantic sensibility, where Switzerland appears as the idyllic place of an unspoiled nature and humanity, and the homeland of all republican virtues. And yet, at the same time, Goethe notes in his Letters Written from Switzerland that the myth of Swiss liberty is merely an "old children's tale preserved in spirits of wine," and another German traveler, Christian Hirschfeld, complains in 1776 about the immorality and drunkenness of the Swiss.

Caricatures

We have undoubtedly not finished living with this kind of contradictory images where truth and fiction, idealizing clichés and grotesque caricatures mix and intertwine in a disconcerting way, whether they are auto-stereotypes or hetero-stereotypes—that is, "type" portraits painted by the Swiss themselves or seen from the outside. This ranges, as Georges-André Chevallaz says, "from the triumphal march to twelve-tone music." And while most of our politicians and official orators still have the unfortunate tendency to emphasize that there is no one like us, the majority of writers, a true "extra-parliamentary opposition," constantly reminds us that we live in a selfish society, in the paradise of materialism and sterile conformity.

As for foreign observers, we must admit that they are less and less inclined, and for good reason, to identify us with the open, hospitable, and courageous country whose memory we would like to perpetuate...

In this regard, a recent publication by the New Helvetic Society entitled Switzerland and the World is full of interest. Not only because it raises the problem of our integration into a Europe that is, after all, being built without us and almost against us (we will not forget that in 1992 customs barriers are to fall), but because it offers us a series of images of Switzerland that give us food for thought.

Thus the Frenchman Lionel Richard, who observes that "the few positive aspects that the image of Switzerland could present in France have deteriorated" and who questions "this astonishing compartmentalization" of French-speaking Switzerland. Or Helmut-Maria Glogger, a German journalist living in Zurich, who, while declaring "I love Switzerland," stigmatizes our self-satisfaction. Against this self-satisfaction, the Basel writer Urs Widmer advocates for prolonged stays abroad, himself a Swiss from abroad who returned home where he rediscovers our national symbol, the cow.

Other Swiss writers are more aggressive; Claude Jaquillard declares, "It is better to be European, alive, revolutionary, and conquering than Swiss, neutral, protected, provident, and dead," while the Ticinese Dante Andrea Franzetti, holder of two passports, claims his Italian heritage against a narrow "Swissness."

Flaw of the System

There are, of course, more balanced opinions, and the former federal councilor does not fail to advocate for the "reasonable and constant osmosis between economy and politics" that others consider the flaw of our system. But it is not certain that even Mr. Chevallaz's good conscience is without flaw. Why would he speak of "the weight of a social conformity sometimes heavier than that of the laws"?

The opinions expressed in these testimonies are far from unanimous. Nevertheless, the image of a country in an identity crisis emerges. Is this a fiction of literary people (yet another one) or reality? The question is posed; there is no way to avoid it.

M. G.

**Announced Performances for Tuesday at 8:30 PM, at the regular rate.** *The Tales of Hoffmann.* Mademoiselle Aquila will sing again this evening, in French, the triple role of Olympia, Giulietta, and Antonia in *The Tales of Hoffmann*. At her side, Mr. Denizot.

**The Comedy** — Announced for every evening at 8:30 PM: *The Squall*, by Bernstein. The summer of June 1914. Reformation Hall.

**Wednesday, February 23rd and Saturday, February 26th, at 8:15 PM, the irrevocably final performances.** Tickets at Rotschy.

**The Art Revue** — St. Peter's Casino. Thursday, February 24th and Sunday, February 27th, at 8:15 PM. Tickets at Messrs. Véron, Grauer and Co., Passage du Terraillet.

**Forest Festival** — Meeting Hall of the Faubourg House, Wednesday the 23rd of this month, at 8:30 PM. Second performance. Tickets available at Rotschy.

**Casino Theatre on Carouge Street.** Performance at 8:30 PM: *The Heir of the Bal Tabarin*.

**Switzerland in Zigzags** — The Geneva City Gymnastic Singers are organizing, with the participation of Mr. Stalder from Bern, an evening of luminous projections which will be held in the Reformation Hall on March 2nd next. Mr. Stalder has already given numerous lectures of this kind with the greatest success in French-speaking Switzerland, France, and Belgium. It is as a true artist, in love with the Alps, that Mr. Stalder has patiently collected the splendid collection of colored slides, by means of which he will take us on a zigzag tour through the Alpine cantons. The session will be enhanced by various solos and patriotic or descriptive choruses (60 performers). In accordance with a tradition dear to them, the Gymnastic Singers wish to associate a charitable work with their evening: this year they have chosen the hospital for sick children on Gourgas Street, and they hope that the public, by filling all the seats in the Reformation Hall, will allow them to bring some relief to the very heavy burdens weighing on this so useful and so deserving institution.

**Announced Concerts** Thursday, February 24th, 8:30 PM, Reformation Hall, thirteenth popular concert of the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande, under the direction of Mr. Ernest Ansermet and with the participation of Mr. Morel, cellist.

completion:
Mr. Pichon in Madrid.
Mr. Pichon, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, has arrived in Madrid. Today, he will dine with the king. Various festivities are planned in his honor.

The correspondent of Le Temps in Spain telegraphs that in Madrid, great importance is attached to Mr. Pichon's visit. Political, financial, and military circles believe that a decisive moment in Moroccan affairs is approaching. It is thought that, given the Moroccan agitation against the police organization, energetic action could prevent many violent incidents, and it is expected that from the conferences Mr. Pichon will hold with the king and his ministers, a more active combined action by France and Spain will result.

General d'Amade arrived on Monday morning at ten o'clock in Casablanca and immediately took command of the troops of the occupation corps.

Dispatch from Casablanca.
It is reported from Casablanca:
Our troops have returned to Casablanca, leaving at the kasbah of Mediouna a battalion of infantry, a squadron of artillery, two machine gun sections, and a cavalry platoon.

As of January 5th, Colonel Boutégoûrd—who served as interim commander between General Drude and General d'Amade—telegraphs that indigenous families are returning in large numbers to Casablanca.

Furthermore, fractions of tribes presented themselves on January 3rd at the kasbah of Mediouna to request amnesty (aman). No hostile movements against us are reported in the surrounding areas.

A supply convoy departs from Casablanca to ensure the garrison of the kasbah of Mediouna provisions for eight days of food and 472 cartridges per man.

Against the Beni-Snassen.
A telegram from General Lyautey, dated January 4th, announces that a column consisting of six infantry companies, a mountain artillery section, and the goum, commanded by Colonel Félineau, departed from Aïn-Sfa and swept through the mountainous massif, passing through Kattecha and the Titinies pass, and pushed its advance guard up to Bou-Zabel.

The operation was carried out with great vigor by the troops. The column encountered no resistance from the indigenous people, who have almost fully paid their fines.

The health condition of the troops leaves nothing to be desired.
The operations against the Beni-Snassen can be considered as successfully concluded.

General Lyautey has telegraphed to thank the government for the congratulations addressed to him. He attributes these congratulations to his troops, whose bravery and endurance ensured the success of the operations he directed.

Those reinforcement troops that had been taken from Tunisia to augment General Lyautey's expeditionary corps will be returned to Tunisia.

The Franco-Spanish Police.
It is reported from Tangier, January 6th, to Le Temps:
The rumors regarding the agitation that the installation of police in the ports would produce among Moroccans are somewhat exaggerated.

In Mazagan, Safi, Mogador, where the police is French, no difficulties have arisen so far.

In Rabat, when the French officers began taking measures for the functioning of the police, some Moroccan officials tried to incite the population; but their intrigues having been discovered and denounced, the unfavorable talk by the populace suddenly ceased.

In Tetuan, the agitation had a more serious character. Upon the arrival of the Spanish officers, several indigenous notables and some religious leaders went to the governor to protest against the installation of the police, claiming that the hostility of the city's population and surrounding tribes against this reform could provoke serious disorders.

They added to support their opinion that a neighboring tribe, called the Beni-Hezmar, had already, as a protest against the police, ceased attending the city market.

The governor replied that he could only comply with the Sultan's orders. After a rather heated discussion, it was decided that the protesters' protest would be brought to the attention of Torres, the Sultan's representative in Tangier.

There have been no other disturbances in Tetuan.
It should also be noted that the agitation of the indigenous people against the police or other reforms is never spontaneous. The subordinate agents of the makhzen almost always foment it covertly, less out of fanaticism than because any reform implies foreign oversight that hinders their administrative practices.

It must also be considered that despite the real evolution that has occurred in the mindset of the makhzen, these methods are not viewed unfavorably by some of its members, who, given their need for our support, pretend to align with our views but secretly attempt a final effort to thwart the reforms.

Notice. Advertisements to be inserted in this newspaper, which are not delivered to the office by Tuesday morning at nine o'clock at the latest, will be irrevocably postponed to the next issue.

OFFICIAL ARTICLES.

1. The public is informed that, by the benefit of a gracious decree of the Lordship and a directive sentence of the honorable Justice of La Chaux-de-Fonds, the guardian and relatives of the children of Henri Jean-Maire will appear in the court of Justice of said La Chaux-de-Fonds on Tuesday, September 5th, at the ordinary session, at the usual place and time, to petition on behalf of the children born and to be born of said Henri Jean-Maire and Reine, born Robert-Nicoud, husband and wife, a formal and legal renunciation of the present and future assets and debts of their said father and mother. Therefore, all creditors of the latter who believe they have grounds for opposition to said petition for renunciation may appear and assert their rights as they deem best, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of La Chaux-de-Fonds.

2. The government having granted to Henriette, daughter of the late Captain Lieutenant Jacques Henri Bourquin, widow of Jacob, son of Jacques Guye, of Les Verrières, resident and parishioner of La Côte-aux-Fées, permission to put her assets into foreclosure; all her creditors are hereby required to meet at said Les Verrières, at the seat of Justice, before Mr. Charles Cousandier, mayor of said place, and the assessors appointed by him, on Monday, September 5th next, furnished with their titles and claims, in order to be registered and then ranked according to their order and dates, under penalty of foreclosure. Issued by order at the clerk's office of Les Verrières, August 15, 1808. H. F. Jeanjaquet, clerk.

3. The public is informed that Mr. Charles-Henri Bonvêpre and Miss Julie-Valérie Bonvêpre, son and daughter of the late Mr. Charles-Guillaume Bonvêpre, member of the Grand Council and hospitalier, and of Mrs. Susanne Petitpierre, his widow, citizen of Neuchatel, have been admitted by decree of the Council of State dated July 5th last, to petition a formal and legal renunciation of the present and future assets and debts of their said father and mother. Consequently, they will appear before the noble Court of Justice of Neuchatel, which will assemble in the town hall of this city, on Friday, September 23rd current, at the usual hour of the session, a day on which all those who could oppose said petition for renunciation are peremptorily summoned to appear in said Justice to uphold their rights, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of Neuchatel.

4. The estate of the late church elder Jonas Besançon, of Engolon, having been declared vacant to the Lordship, its liquidation has been ordered and set for Friday, September 8th current. And Henri Favre, of Villard, and his wife Jeanne-Marie, born Morel, widow of Jean-Daniel Favre, having obtained the discussion of their assets to satisfy their debts, which has also been set for Wednesday, September 7th of said month: All creditors whatsoever of these two estates, including those of the said widow from her first marriage, are required to appear on the aforementioned days before the Mayor of Valangin and the appointed assessors, around eight o'clock in the morning, to assert their claims and be ranked according to law, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of Valangin.

5. Marianne Perrenoud, of La Sagne, daughter of the late Jacob Perrenoud and Judith, born Jaquet, died July 27th and buried July 29th of the same month in Neuchatel, having by her testament of August 7th, 1798, called as heirs of her assets her relatives descended from siblings, stating: "I create and appoint as my sole and unique heirs in all my assets my cousins removed from siblings, without exception, not knowing them all by their names, on condition that they settle, etc. etc." And said relatives possibly not all being known, they are advised by this notice that Friday, September 9th current, is the final day on which the possession and investiture of the assets of the deceased must be claimed before the noble Court of Justice, assembled in the town hall, by those of said relatives who are in the country and who deem they have rights to assert. This notice thus given without consequence, given the extraordinary clause above, extracted from the testament of the deceased, which is deposited in original at the clerk's office of Neuchatel, will be inserted three times in this newspaper and announced at the sermon of the church of La Sagne, jurisdiction of the deceased.

AUCTION NOTICES.

6. The commission for the benefit of inventory of the estate of the wagoner Louis Floquet gives notice by these presents that on Tuesday, September 6th next, at nine o'clock in the morning, on the square of Yverdon, four wagons, two carts (one covered), a large and strong wagoner's cart, harnesses, and other items of wagoner's equipment will be exposed for sale by public auction under conditions that will be read. Given at Yverdon, August 23rd, 1808. Auberjosois, president. 25. F. Corevoit, clerk.

7. By permission obtained, the Four Ministers will expose for auction on September 23rd current, at the conclusion of the session, a vineyard of about two workers and a quarter, including the old Honhomme alley adjoining, situated at Plan de Serrière, between the old road of said Serrière d'ubère, the new road leading to the bridge of Joran, the vineyard of Captain Jacobel de Vent. This vineyard is largely surrounded by a wall, and it will be exposed for auction with its harvest and under conditions that will be read before said auction.

8. Following permission obtained, two carriages, saddles, harnesses, horse collars, and other items of this kind will be exposed for public auction on Friday, September 9th current, at ten o'clock in the morning, before the house De Charrière, at the bottom of the village of Colombier.

9. Following permission obtained, the following pieces forming part of the domain belonging to the late Mr. De Charrière, within the jurisdiction of Colombier, will be exposed for auction in Justice of Colombier on Wednesday, November 2nd next: 1. a property called La Mairesse, situated between Bôle and Colombier, containing 8 poses 7 perches, furnished with fruit trees, with house and fountain; 2. a field at Preyla, containing about 2 poses; 3. two vineyards at Chatenaya, planted in red, together containing 18 workers.

10. Messieurs Jean-David Mauley and Jean Confesse, justices, acting as joint curators of the estate of the late Félix Tinembart and as syndics of the mass of its discussion, advise the public that they will expose for public auction under reasonable conditions, in Justice at Bevaix, on September 16th next, at ten o'clock in the morning, a superb house built at the bottom of the village of said place, on the road to Neuchatel, consisting of three distinct dwellings, a ground-floor bakery, a barn, a cellar, an oil mill with the appurtenances, orchard and adjoining garden, containing one pose and a quarter, and where there is a plantation of fine trees of several species; plus, and finally, a superb balance with the stones. Interested parties may address themselves before the auction to the aforementioned syndics to take knowledge of all these items. Given at the clerk's office of Bevaix, August 23rd, 1808. By order: J. J. Pernet, clerk.

OFFERED FOR SALE.

11. Mr. Roy, having decided at the request of several persons to sell parcels of a light wine of about eight bosses, vintage 1802, offers it at the price of five batz per pot, taking at least 100 pots; he will deliver samples to interested parties and receive their subscriptions. This wine leaves nothing to be desired in quality, but it leaves the seller regrets over the lowness of the price.
