Notice. Advertisements to be inserted in this newspaper, which are not delivered to the office by Tuesday morning at nine o'clock at the latest, will be irrevocably postponed to the next issue.

OFFICIAL ARTICLES.

1. The public is informed that, by the benefit of a gracious decree of the Lordship and a directive sentence of the honorable Justice of La Chaux-de-Fonds, the guardian and relatives of the children of Henri Jean-Maire will appear in the court of Justice of said La Chaux-de-Fonds on Tuesday, September 5th, at the ordinary session, at the usual place and time, to petition on behalf of the children born and to be born of said Henri Jean-Maire and Reine, born Robert-Nicoud, husband and wife, a formal and legal renunciation of the present and future assets and debts of their said father and mother. Therefore, all creditors of the latter who believe they have grounds for opposition to said petition for renunciation may appear and assert their rights as they deem best, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of La Chaux-de-Fonds.

2. The government having granted to Henriette, daughter of the late Captain Lieutenant Jacques Henri Bourquin, widow of Jacob, son of Jacques Guye, of Les Verrières, resident and parishioner of La Côte-aux-Fées, permission to put her assets into foreclosure; all her creditors are hereby required to meet at said Les Verrières, at the seat of Justice, before Mr. Charles Cousandier, mayor of said place, and the assessors appointed by him, on Monday, September 5th next, furnished with their titles and claims, in order to be registered and then ranked according to their order and dates, under penalty of foreclosure. Issued by order at the clerk's office of Les Verrières, August 15, 1808. H. F. Jeanjaquet, clerk.

3. The public is informed that Mr. Charles-Henri Bonvêpre and Miss Julie-Valérie Bonvêpre, son and daughter of the late Mr. Charles-Guillaume Bonvêpre, member of the Grand Council and hospitalier, and of Mrs. Susanne Petitpierre, his widow, citizen of Neuchatel, have been admitted by decree of the Council of State dated July 5th last, to petition a formal and legal renunciation of the present and future assets and debts of their said father and mother. Consequently, they will appear before the noble Court of Justice of Neuchatel, which will assemble in the town hall of this city, on Friday, September 23rd current, at the usual hour of the session, a day on which all those who could oppose said petition for renunciation are peremptorily summoned to appear in said Justice to uphold their rights, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of Neuchatel.

4. The estate of the late church elder Jonas Besançon, of Engolon, having been declared vacant to the Lordship, its liquidation has been ordered and set for Friday, September 8th current. And Henri Favre, of Villard, and his wife Jeanne-Marie, born Morel, widow of Jean-Daniel Favre, having obtained the discussion of their assets to satisfy their debts, which has also been set for Wednesday, September 7th of said month: All creditors whatsoever of these two estates, including those of the said widow from her first marriage, are required to appear on the aforementioned days before the Mayor of Valangin and the appointed assessors, around eight o'clock in the morning, to assert their claims and be ranked according to law, under penalty of foreclosure. Clerk's office of Valangin.

5. Marianne Perrenoud, of La Sagne, daughter of the late Jacob Perrenoud and Judith, born Jaquet, died July 27th and buried July 29th of the same month in Neuchatel, having by her testament of August 7th, 1798, called as heirs of her assets her relatives descended from siblings, stating: "I create and appoint as my sole and unique heirs in all my assets my cousins removed from siblings, without exception, not knowing them all by their names, on condition that they settle, etc. etc." And said relatives possibly not all being known, they are advised by this notice that Friday, September 9th current, is the final day on which the possession and investiture of the assets of the deceased must be claimed before the noble Court of Justice, assembled in the town hall, by those of said relatives who are in the country and who deem they have rights to assert. This notice thus given without consequence, given the extraordinary clause above, extracted from the testament of the deceased, which is deposited in original at the clerk's office of Neuchatel, will be inserted three times in this newspaper and announced at the sermon of the church of La Sagne, jurisdiction of the deceased.

AUCTION NOTICES.

6. The commission for the benefit of inventory of the estate of the wagoner Louis Floquet gives notice by these presents that on Tuesday, September 6th next, at nine o'clock in the morning, on the square of Yverdon, four wagons, two carts (one covered), a large and strong wagoner's cart, harnesses, and other items of wagoner's equipment will be exposed for sale by public auction under conditions that will be read. Given at Yverdon, August 23rd, 1808. Auberjosois, president. 25. F. Corevoit, clerk.

7. By permission obtained, the Four Ministers will expose for auction on September 23rd current, at the conclusion of the session, a vineyard of about two workers and a quarter, including the old Honhomme alley adjoining, situated at Plan de Serrière, between the old road of said Serrière d'ubère, the new road leading to the bridge of Joran, the vineyard of Captain Jacobel de Vent. This vineyard is largely surrounded by a wall, and it will be exposed for auction with its harvest and under conditions that will be read before said auction.

8. Following permission obtained, two carriages, saddles, harnesses, horse collars, and other items of this kind will be exposed for public auction on Friday, September 9th current, at ten o'clock in the morning, before the house De Charrière, at the bottom of the village of Colombier.

9. Following permission obtained, the following pieces forming part of the domain belonging to the late Mr. De Charrière, within the jurisdiction of Colombier, will be exposed for auction in Justice of Colombier on Wednesday, November 2nd next: 1. a property called La Mairesse, situated between Bôle and Colombier, containing 8 poses 7 perches, furnished with fruit trees, with house and fountain; 2. a field at Preyla, containing about 2 poses; 3. two vineyards at Chatenaya, planted in red, together containing 18 workers.

10. Messieurs Jean-David Mauley and Jean Confesse, justices, acting as joint curators of the estate of the late Félix Tinembart and as syndics of the mass of its discussion, advise the public that they will expose for public auction under reasonable conditions, in Justice at Bevaix, on September 16th next, at ten o'clock in the morning, a superb house built at the bottom of the village of said place, on the road to Neuchatel, consisting of three distinct dwellings, a ground-floor bakery, a barn, a cellar, an oil mill with the appurtenances, orchard and adjoining garden, containing one pose and a quarter, and where there is a plantation of fine trees of several species; plus, and finally, a superb balance with the stones. Interested parties may address themselves before the auction to the aforementioned syndics to take knowledge of all these items. Given at the clerk's office of Bevaix, August 23rd, 1808. By order: J. J. Pernet, clerk.

OFFERED FOR SALE.

11. Mr. Roy, having decided at the request of several persons to sell parcels of a light wine of about eight bosses, vintage 1802, offers it at the price of five batz per pot, taking at least 100 pots; he will deliver samples to interested parties and receive their subscriptions. This wine leaves nothing to be desired in quality, but it leaves the seller regrets over the lowness of the price.

French Film
To those who might believe that "The Shark" was produced according to the so-called "international" formula, it is worth recalling that the director Henri Chomette, in writing his screenplay, gave it a distinctly French character, and that he filmed it in the intended atmosphere. This is how we will see Le Havre, Rouen and its Palace of Justice, and those banks of the Seine which, in springtime, become enchanting. "The Shark," recorded using the European Tobis-Klang-Film processes, is therefore, without question, the first talking and sound film made under the French sky.

Sound Equipment
We learn that the Aenesmann company, owner of the Palais de la Mutualité, after having studied the various sound projection devices existing on the French market, has decided to adopt the Klang-Film-Tobis equipment for its incomparable qualities, both in terms of sound reproduction and its construction. Our congratulations to Messrs. Davidson and Aenesmann, who know so wisely how to follow progress.

Spain. Madrid, September 6. Mr. Carnero, former secretary of our embassy in Paris, arrived here two days ago, carrying important dispatches. Rumors have since spread that France and England have united to impress upon Spain the absolute necessity of reforming our current system of government. Desertion in our army is becoming alarming. The ministry is positively informed by official reports from the governors of Extremadura and Galicia that desertion has, to date, taken 3,400 men from the Spanish army, of whom 2,000 have entered Portugal through Portuguese Extremadura, known as Alentejo, and 1,400 through the province of Tras-os-Montes. EXTRACT FROM OUR CORRESPONDENCE.
Corfu, 6 June.

An English warship, which departed ten days ago from Naples for Germany, arrived this morning in our port. We learn from it that the current government is handling affairs with the greatest activity, especially regarding the supply of fortresses. A large quantity of grain from the island of Syros has arrived in this city. Various shipments of the same kind have been dispatched from Zakynthos. If, as hoped, the enemy cannot penetrate the countryside of Argos, the harvest from that region will be sufficient for some time. Moreover, the government is constantly working to assemble troops in order to oppose the enemy's plans. It is said that Rumeli Valessi is preparing to march against Athens, and that four thousand men have departed for Salona under the command of his lieutenant.

We also learn that the enemy, taking advantage of the initial terror spread throughout Greece by the fall of Missolonghi, had offered favorable terms to the remnants of its garrison; that spies had infiltrated the Greek camp to influence minds, and that one of them, named Basile Barlas, sent back twice to his master, finally paid with his head for a third and futile attempt. There is no longer any doubt that about two thousand individuals escaped the disaster of Missolonghi, including 1,600 men fit to bear arms, and the rest women and girls. The latter have gone to the Peloponnese to seek refuge with the government; the others are at Kravari (in Locris) joined with other Greek leaders who guard the passes of that province.

Neither Ibrahim, who after heading toward Kalavryta was forced to fall back on Patras, nor Chutaehi, who was in western Greece, have undertaken any operations, so weakened have they been by the losses their troops suffered before Missolonghi. The Turkish fleet was encountered in the Archipelago, heading toward Constantinople. The Egyptian fleet is at Modon.

Electoral Geography and Its Aspects
ON THE EVE OF THE VOTE
(Special Correspondence)
Bern, October 24.

On Monday, we extensively outlined the general aspects of the fierce struggle that is brewing and showed how differences in tendencies and nuances are merging within bourgeois or national parties to concentrate offensive and defensive efforts on a single front: that of social order and democracy.

The few days that have passed since, days rich in electoral agitation, saturated with political declamations, and flooded with incendiary pamphlets, have only strengthened national wills and reinforced all bourgeois positions against the common adversary: the far-left.

In federal political circles, there is optimism—reasonably, we think—about the outcome of the great battle underway. Both radical federal councillors and their Catholic colleagues expect a strengthening of their respective positions through the partial success of their troops. It is anticipated either a radical advance in Bern, Zurich, St. Gall, and Grisons, or a conservative advance in Zurich, Schwyz, perhaps St. Gall, and perhaps Valais. Regardless of the success of the socialist list, it is generally agreed that it will not suffice to provide Marx's disciples with the major moral victory of conquering a relative majority in Parliament. The electorate as a whole has finally understood that by cutting the roots and attacking the trunk of the national economic tree, branches, leaves, and fruits would inevitably wither.

Basel-City sends to Bern four bourgeois and three extremists. An "evangelical" party is intervening this time in the fray and has refused to ally with other national parties. This strange attitude is causing concerns about the outcome of the vote in the large city on the Rhine, and there is fear that evangelicalism may serve as a springboard for the Moscow followers, which would be deeply regrettable.

Basel-Country is fertile in dissenters and troublemakers. There is concern that the electoral whims of certain opportunists fishing in troubled waters may prove fatal to the radicals.

No change is expected in Solothurn, which sends to Bern 3 radicals, 2 Catholics, and 2 socialists; nor in Aargau, whose current delegation includes 3 Catholics, 3 farmers, 4 socialists, and 2 radicals; nor in Ticino, which delights in constantly reshuffling its delegation personnel without altering the numerical importance of the represented parties.

Three enclaves of peace within the electoral furnace: Glarus, a happy country, which tacitly re-elects its excellent radical deputy; Outer Appenzell, a land of bliss, which proclaims elected without any contest its two radicals and its socialist; and finally Inner Appenzell, a classic island of unalterable federalism, which imperturbably refuses "everything that comes from Bern" and considers it unnecessary to disturb its voters for such a minor matter.

In Neuchâtel, there is no regret over the lamentable crumbling of the Catholic list, an absurdity of ill-fated inspiration and foreign import, and it is hoped that this unfortunate dissent will not harm, in the final count, the national cause.

In Fribourg, the struggle is extremely fierce, thanks to the entry into the scene, for the first time, of a "farmers, artisans, and bourgeois" party. This new electoral constellation could well record an immediate first success, but no one can predict whether the seat conquered will be taken from the majority party or from the radicals.

Things seem likely to proceed much more calmly in the canton of Vaud, where no notable change is expected, and in Geneva, where a decline for the democrats in favor of the economic defense party is generally anticipated. It is Mr. de Rabours whom everyone already delivers to the fatal blade of the dry guillotine. If such a prediction proves accurate, Parliament would lose one of its most sympathetic figures and one of its best orators, at a time when disciples of Demosthenes in Bern are almost counted on one hand!... B.

entre M. participation de la Suisse à l'action internationale d'octroi de crédits à l'Europe centrale.Le message indique tout d'abord qu'en ce qui concerne fl. es livraisons, l'action de secours est SWISS CONFEDERATION INTERNATIONAL OFFICES.— The Federal Council has appointed Mr. Arthur Redard of Echandens, previously deputy, as registrar of the International Register of Trademarks and Commerce.

FEDERAL SUBSIDIES.— The Confederation has allocated the following subsidies: To the canton of Fribourg: 25% of the sanitation costs in the communes of Marsens and Sorens (estimate 81,400 francs, maximum 20,350 francs). To the canton of Valais: a) 25% of the costs for completing the "Bitscheri" water pipeline in the commune of Bitsch (estimate 50,000 francs, maximum 12,500 francs). b) 25% of the costs for constructing two barns on the "Schafalpe" in the commune of Ems (estimate 28,000 francs, maximum 7,000 francs).

PRECIOUS METALS.— According to a communication from the Federal Bureau for Gold and Silver Materials, the following markings were carried out by the control offices during the third quarter of 1921: gold watch cases, 80,195 (252,924 in 1920); silver watch cases, 146,953 (291,761 in 1920); platinum watch cases, 1,302 (1,247 in 1920); gold, silver, and platinum jewelry and silverware items, 214,843 (313,846 in 1920), controlled or verified.

SWISS LIVING ABROAD.— The Federal Council has voted a new credit of 100,000 francs to assist Swiss citizens returned from abroad who are in difficult circumstances.

Furthermore, the Federal Council has definitively approved the statutes of the Swiss Hotel Trust Society. This society is thus able to begin its activities immediately.

APPRENTICES.— The Swiss Association for Career Choice and Apprentice Protection, which held its 18th annual assembly in Lucerne, has decided to publish a special bulletin for apprentice placements. The revision of the statutes will include the creation of a permanent secretariat and an increase in annual contributions.

ON THE MARITIME UNION.— We are informed that, contrary to agency information, no decision whatsoever has been taken by the inquiry commission charged with examining the management of the Maritime Union. The examination of the accounts is not yet completed, and all news published on this subject is inaccurate.

TELEGRAPH FORMS.— The General Directorate of Telegraphs has decided to print advertisements on telegram forms written by the sender or delivered to recipients, as well as on dispatch envelopes. It would thus save the cost of paper and could provide forms free of charge to all interested parties.

Socialists and Customs Tariffs Solothurn, October 3. The socialists organized a protest meeting on Sunday against the customs tariff, wage reductions, and unemployment. Mr. Schneider, State Councillor of Basel, and Mr. Staehli, worker secretary from Bern, delivered speeches.

Switzerland-Denmark Copenhagen, October 3. An exchange of views took place in Copenhagen between Mr. Bosshardt of the Swiss Commercial Exchange and the two secretaries of the Copenhagen Chamber of Commerce regarding the development of trade between Denmark and Switzerland, and specifically the reciprocal abolition of monopolies. Mr. Bosshardt offered his services to Danish merchants for all commercial information. Mr. Bosshardt visited all the facilities of the Copenhagen Exchange.

Aid to Austria Bern, October 3. The Federal Council today publishes its message to the Federal Assembly on Switzerland's participation in the international action to grant credits to Central Europe. The message first indicates that, concerning relief deliveries, the relief action is currently concluded for Switzerland. The Food Office has supplied Austria with goods valued at 23,911,281 francs; to this must be added a sum of 1 million francs for the repatriation of prisoners of war from Russia. The International Credit Commission having proposed the Ter Meulen system as the basis for Austria's reconstruction, which is only applicable if all creditors of this country agree to an extension of the payment deadline for capital and interest, and furthermore renounce their mortgage rights, France, Great Britain, Japan, and Italy decided to renounce, even for reconstruction credits and for a period yet to be determined, the priority rights they held. Switzerland was, on this occasion, requested to renounce its priority rights as well. In its session of September 2, 1921, the Federal Council decided to adhere to the renunciation declaration presented to it, provided that this was also accepted by all other states participating in the relief action and subject to approval of the decision by the Federal Chambers. It today proposes to the Chambers to approve said decision. The Federal Council's message contains the text of the renunciation declaration requested from Switzerland, which stipulates, besides relinquishing the priority right that the federal government commits not to claim before June 1, 1941, no payment of any kind whatsoever related to relief bonds already issued or to be issued in the future by the Austrian government.

Divorce and Separation The Federal Council addresses to the Federal Assembly a report on the Schmid motion regarding revision of the Hague Convention of June 12, 1902 regulating conflicts of laws and jurisdiction in matters of divorce and separation. The revision requested by the motion aims to allow a Swiss woman married to a foreigner to request divorce even in cases where it is only permitted under Swiss law, and in any case when the marriage was celebrated in Switzerland and the woman has been reinstated in Swiss nationality. The Federal Council proposes not to proceed with the matter.

Farmers' Union In its ordinary assembly held Monday in the large hall of the Casino in Bern, under the presidency of Mr. Jenny, National Councillor in Bern, the Swiss Farmers' Union re-elected its president by acclamation and then proceeded to elect its committee, which comprises 80 members. 74 were re-elected. The six new members are Mr. Blanc, secretary of the Vaud Chamber of Agriculture; Donini of Lugano; Honegger of Dürnten (Zurich); Kramer of Lurtigen (Fribourg); Roth of Bern; Steiner, National Councillor, of Kaltbrunn (St. Gallen).

Administration of the Swiss Federal Railways Bern, October 3. The board of administration of the Swiss Federal Railways approved a supply contract for 15,800 tons of cast steel rails, solid rails for switch blades, and metal sleepers for the price of 2 million francs, rounded. It discussed the report of the general management and the permanent commission regarding the method of covering the expenses of the pension and relief fund borne by the administration. According to the proposal of the general management and the permanent commission, the administration of the Swiss Federal Railways would provide its share of the fund's expenses in this manner: 1) It would pay an annual contribution of 7% of the eligible income, increased to 7.5% for locomotive personnel; starting January 1, 1924, this contribution would increase each year by 1% of the total annual income until it reaches respectively 11% and 11.5%. 2) It would pay to the fund a sum equal to 5 monthly factors of each increase in annual eligible income. 3) On the day when these contributions added to the other annual resources of the fund no longer suffice to cover the annual expenses, the operating account would bear the deficit. The board of administration agreed with this view. To a question from a board member, the general management responded that the laying of the double track Solothurn-Longeau is also included in the program of works to be undertaken to combat unemployment, for which the Federal Council will request the necessary credits at the next session of the Federal Assembly.

An exchange of views took place in Copenhagen between Mr. Bosshardt of the Swiss Commercial Exchange and the two secretaries of the Copenhagen Chamber of Commerce regarding the development of trade between Denmark and Switzerland, and specifically the reciprocal abolition of monopolies. Mr. Bosshardt offered his services to Danish merchants for all commercial information. Mr. Bosshardt visited all the facilities of the Copenhagen Exchange.

Aid to Austria Bern, October 3. The Federal Council today publishes its message to the Federal Assembly on Switzerland's participation in the international action to grant credits to Central Europe. The message first indicates that, concerning relief deliveries, the relief action is currently concluded for Switzerland. The Food Office has supplied Austria with goods valued at 23,911,281 francs; to this must be added a sum of 1 million francs for the repatriation of prisoners of war from Russia. The International Credit Commission having proposed the Ter Meulen system as the basis for Austria's reconstruction, which is only applicable if all creditors of this country agree to an extension of the payment deadline for capital and interest, and furthermore renounce their mortgage rights, France, Great Britain, Japan, and Italy decided to renounce, even for reconstruction credits and for a period yet to be determined, the priority rights they held. Switzerland was, on this occasion, requested to renounce its priority rights as well. In its session of September 2, 1921, the Federal Council decided to adhere to the renunciation declaration presented to it, provided that this was also accepted by all other states participating in the relief action and subject to approval of the decision by the Federal Chambers. It today proposes to the Chambers to approve said decision. The Federal Council's message contains the text of the renunciation declaration requested from Switzerland, which stipulates, besides relinquishing the priority right that the federal government commits not to claim before June 1, 1941, no payment of any kind whatsoever related to relief bonds already issued or to be issued in the future by the Austrian government.

Divorce and Separation The Federal Council addresses to the Federal Assembly a report on the Schmid motion regarding revision of the Hague Convention of June 12, 1902 regulating conflicts of laws and jurisdiction in matters of divorce and separation. The revision requested by the motion aims to allow a Swiss woman married to a foreigner to request divorce even in cases where it is only permitted under Swiss law, and in any case when the marriage was celebrated in Switzerland and the woman has been reinstated in Swiss nationality. The Federal Council proposes not to proceed with the matter.

Farmers' Union In its ordinary assembly held Monday in the large hall of the Casino in Bern, under the presidency of Mr. Jenny, National Councillor in Bern, the Swiss Farmers' Union re-elected its president by acclamation and then proceeded to elect its committee, which comprises 80 members. 74 were re-elected. The six new members are Mr. Blanc, secretary of the Vaud Chamber of Agriculture; Donini of Lugano; Honegger of Dürnten (Zurich); Kramer of Lurtigen (Fribourg); Roth of Bern; Steiner, National Councillor, of Kaltbrunn (St. Gallen).

Administration of the Swiss Federal Railways Bern, October 3. The board of administration of the Swiss Federal Railways approved a supply contract for 15,800 tons of cast steel rails, solid rails for switch blades, and metal sleepers for the price of 2 million francs, rounded. It discussed the report of the general management and the permanent commission regarding the method of covering the expenses of the pension and relief fund borne by the administration. According to the proposal of the general management and the permanent commission, the administration of the Swiss Federal Railways would provide its share of the fund's expenses in this manner: 1) It would pay an annual contribution of 7% of the eligible income, increased to 7.5% for locomotive personnel; starting January 1, 1924, this contribution would increase each year by 1% of the total annual income until it reaches respectively 11% and 11.5%. 2) It would pay to the fund a sum equal to 5 monthly factors of each increase in annual eligible income. 3) On the day when these contributions added to the other annual resources of the fund no longer suffice to cover the annual expenses, the operating account would bear the deficit. The board of administration agreed with this view. To a question from a board member, the general management responded that the laying of the double track Solothurn-Longeau is also included in the program of works to be undertaken to combat unemployment, for which the Federal Council will request the necessary credits at the next session of the Federal Assembly.

THE 24 HOURS by Serge Lang  
The Bad Argument  
Rik van Looy is not happy. The world road champion declared: "If the organizers do not modify the route of the 1962 Tour de France, I will not participate." A few hours earlier, the Tour organizers, tired by the multiple indiscretions of recent weeks, had published the route of the great Tour: 22 stages, no rest days, four time trial stages (including one team time trial), totaling 4173 km.  

"Four time trials?" exclaimed the Belgian. "So they want to make Anquetil win at any cost? If that's how it is, I withdraw..."  

The Belgian champion's stance did not fail to unpleasantly surprise the organizers. Indeed, until now, Rik van Looy had never agreed to come and participate in the "grand loop." Each time, Rik had claimed that with the national team formula, he would not find the necessary support within the "Belgian squadron," whose members, inevitably, would be jealous rivals rather than stylish "water carriers."  

With the formula of the event changed, Rik this time had good reasons to accept this participation offered to him on a silver platter. Far from it... Even before the details of the route were known, we had learned that Rik van Looy was frowning. After careful consideration, he now regretted that good old formula of national teams. Moreover, he is not alone. He believed that with the Belgian team from the World Championships, which he had so generously paid for its members to help him retain his title, his chances would have been greater.  

Then came the issue of the time trial stages. Personally, I believe that four time trial stages harm the overall interest of a Tour. As for the team time trial stage, coincidentally organized in Herentals, Rik van Looy's village, it is a bad joke that one would have hoped not to see again in an event as important as the Tour.  

But between our opinion and van Looy's "veto," there is a gap. The organizers are the sole judges. Van Looy, not content with earning 800,000 Swiss francs per season, would like the Tour to be tailored to him... Never did the great Coppi, Kubler, Koblet, or Louison Bobet have such an insolent and ridiculous pretension at once.  

Fortunately, the organizers refused to consider modifying even one kilometer of the Tour as they conceived it. They did well. If van Looy does not accept it, we will do without him. He will be the loser. Because if one day he wants to be considered equal to Coppi, he will have to start by winning the Tour. He is not yet "there."

GENEVA
Nastassia Kinski:
Work Permit Denied
(ATS).- Actress Nastassia Kinski will not be able to settle in Geneva with her family and establish the company Leila Film SA there, intended to co-produce and promote a film about the life of Henri Dunant, founder of the Red Cross. The Geneva State Council decided on Tuesday not to grant a residence permit and work permit to Nastassia Kinski, stating that "the economic interest of this request was limited."
Last October, the actress submitted a complete application to the population control office. In support of her request, Nastassia Kinski argued that at the time of her second child's birth, she stayed in Geneva where she formed many connections. Nastassia Kinski is also interested in the humanitarian work of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
The State Council rejected this appeal on Tuesday. It notes that the annual quota for workers is quite low and that the available permits are reserved for projects offering significant development opportunities for the Geneva economy, either through the creation or preservation of jobs, through the introduction of new cutting-edge activities, or finally through the revitalization of struggling enterprises.
